chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 1 — Elsinore. A Platform Before the Castle
paragraphs: [Enter Francisco and Barnardo, two sentinels]
BARNARDO. Who's there?
FRANCISCO. No — you answer me first. Stop and identify yourself.
BARNARDO. Long live the King!
FRANCISCO. Barnardo?
BARNARDO. That's me.
FRANCISCO. You're right on time for your shift.
BARNARDO. It's just struck midnight. Get yourself to bed, Francisco.
FRANCISCO. Thanks for relieving me. It's bitterly cold, and I feel sick at heart.
BARNARDO. Has it been a quiet watch?
FRANCISCO. Not a mouse stirring.
BARNARDO. Well, good night. If you run into Horatio and Marcellus, my fellow watchmen, tell them to hurry up.
[Enter Horatio and Marcellus]
FRANCISCO. I think I hear them now. Stop! Who's there?
HORATIO. Friends of this place.
MARCELLUS. And loyal subjects of the King of Denmark.
FRANCISCO. Good night to you.
MARCELLUS. Farewell, honest soldier. Who relieved you?
FRANCISCO. Barnardo has taken my place. Good night.
[Exit.]
MARCELLUS. Hey, Barnardo!
BARNARDO. Is Horatio with you?
HORATIO. More or less.
BARNARDO. Welcome, Horatio. Welcome, good Marcellus.
MARCELLUS. Well? Has that thing appeared again tonight?
BARNARDO. I haven't seen anything.

MARCELLUS. Horatio says it's just our imagination and refuses to believe us about this terrifying sight we've seen twice now. So I asked him to join us on watch tonight, so that if the ghost appears again, he can confirm what our eyes have seen and try to speak to it.
HORATIO. Nonsense, it won't appear.
BARNARDO. Sit down for a moment, and let us try once more to convince you — you who are so resistant to our story — of what we've seen these past two nights.
HORATIO. Fine, let's sit down, and let Barnardo tell us about it.

BARNARDO. Last night, when that same star that sits to the west of the North Star had moved across the sky to light up that same part of the heavens where it's burning now, Marcellus and I, just as the bell was striking one —
MARCELLUS. Quiet, stop! Look — there it comes again.
[Enter Ghost]
BARNARDO. In the same form, looking exactly like the dead King.
MARCELLUS. You're the scholar — speak to it, Horatio.
BARNARDO. Doesn't it look like the King? Look closely, Horatio.
HORATIO. Remarkably so. It fills me with fear and wonder.
BARNARDO. It seems to want someone to speak to it.
MARCELLUS. Talk to it, Horatio.
HORATIO. What are you, claiming this hour of the night, appearing in the fair and warlike form in which the buried King of Denmark once walked among us? By heaven, I command you to speak.
MARCELLUS. It's offended.
BARNARDO. Look — it's walking away.
HORATIO. Wait! Speak, speak! I command you, speak!
[Exit Ghost.]
MARCELLUS. It's gone, and it won't answer.
BARNARDO. What about that, Horatio? You're trembling and pale. Isn't this something more than imagination? What do you make of it?
HORATIO. Before God, I would never have believed this without seeing it with my own eyes.
MARCELLUS. Doesn't it look like the King?

HORATIO. As much as you look like yourself. That was the very armor he wore when he fought the ambitious King of Norway, and that was the same frown he had when, in an angry confrontation, he struck down the Polish forces on the ice. It's strange.
MARCELLUS. Twice before, at exactly this dead hour, it's marched past our watch with that same military stride.
HORATIO. I don't know what to make of it specifically, but in general terms, I think this is a sign that something terrible is coming for our country.

MARCELLUS. Then sit down and tell me — you who know — why we've been put on this strict and constant watch every night, wearing out the people of this land with labor. And why are we casting so many bronze cannons every day, and buying weapons from foreign markets? Why have we pressed shipwrights into such heavy work that they can't tell Sunday from any other day? What's going on that requires this frantic effort, making night work alongside day? Who can tell me?

HORATIO. I can — at least, the rumor goes like this. Our late King, whose image just appeared to us, was challenged to single combat by Fortinbras of Norway, who was driven by fierce competitive pride. Our brave King Hamlet — as the whole world honored him — killed this Fortinbras, who, by a legally sealed agreement, forfeited all the lands he possessed to the conqueror. In return, our King had wagered an equal portion of his own lands, which would have gone to Fortinbras had he won — as the terms of the same contract specified. Now, young Fortinbras — full of untested ambition and hot blood — has been gathering up a ragtag army of lawless mercenaries from the fringes of Norway, feeding them for some bold enterprise. And that enterprise, as our state well knows, is nothing less than taking back by force the lands his father lost. That, I believe, is the main reason for our preparations, the source of this watch, and the chief cause of all the frantic activity in the land.
BARNARDO. I think you're right. It makes sense that this ominous figure would come marching through our watch in armor, looking like the King who was at the center of these wars.

HORATIO. It's a speck that troubles the mind's eye. In Rome at its height, just before the mighty Julius Caesar fell, the graves stood empty and the shrouded dead walked shrieking through the streets. There were stars with trails of fire, bloody dew, disasters in the sun, and the moon — which governs the tides — was eclipsed almost to the point of doomsday. And similar omens, like heralds announcing what fate has in store, have been shown by heaven and earth together to our own land and people.
[Re-enter Ghost]

HORATIO. But wait — look! There it comes again! I'll cross its path, even if it destroys me. Stop, illusion! If you can make any sound or use your voice, speak to me. If there is any good deed that can be done to give you peace and me grace, speak to me. If you know something about our country's fate that, if known in advance, we might prevent — speak! Or if in life you buried stolen treasure in the ground, for which they say spirits often walk after death — tell us about it. Stop and speak!
[The cock crows.]
HORATIO. Stop it, Marcellus!
MARCELLUS. Should I strike it with my weapon?
HORATIO. Yes, if it won't stand still.
BARNARDO. It's here!
HORATIO. It's here!
[Exit Ghost.]
MARCELLUS. It's gone! We were wrong to threaten it — it's so majestic. We were foolish to show it violence. It's as untouchable as the air, and our blows were nothing but mockery.
BARNARDO. It was about to speak when the rooster crowed.

HORATIO. And then it flinched, like a guilty person caught in the act. I've heard that the rooster, which is the trumpet call of morning, wakes the god of day with its loud, clear call, and at that warning, every wandering spirit — whether in sea, fire, earth, or air — hurries back to its place of confinement. And what we just saw proves it.

MARCELLUS. It vanished when the rooster crowed. They say that in the season leading up to Christmas, the rooster sings all night long, and during that time no ghost dares walk abroad. The nights are safe, no planets have malicious influence, no fairy casts spells, and no witch has power to charm — so holy and blessed is that time.

HORATIO. I've heard that too, and I partly believe it. But look — the morning, dressed in reddish brown, is walking over the dew on that hill to the east. Let's end our watch, and I suggest we tell young Hamlet what we've seen tonight. I'm certain this spirit, which was silent with us, will speak to him. Do you agree we should let him know? It's our duty, and our love demands it.
MARCELLUS. Let's do it, please. I know where we can find him this morning.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 2 — Elsinore. A Room of State in the Castle
paragraphs: [Enter Claudius King of Denmark, Gertrude the Queen, Hamlet, Polonius,]
[Laertes, Voltemand,]
[Cornelius, Lords and Attendant]

KING. Though the memory of our dear brother Hamlet's death is still fresh, and it was right for us to grieve with heavy hearts, and for the whole kingdom to wear a look of sorrow — still, wisdom has fought with natural feeling, and we've decided to mourn him with sensible grief while also thinking of ourselves. Therefore, our former sister-in-law, now our queen and co-ruler of this warlike state, we have married — with a kind of defeated joy, one eye weeping and the other smiling, with mirth at the funeral and mourning at the wedding, balancing happiness and sorrow equally. We have not ignored your wise counsel, which has freely supported this decision. We thank you all. Now, you should know that young Fortinbras, thinking little of our strength, or believing our late brother's death has left our state weak and disorganized, has pestered us with messages demanding the surrender of lands his father legally lost to our most valiant brother. So much for him. Now, for ourselves and for this meeting: we have written to the King of Norway, uncle to young Fortinbras — who is old, bedridden, and barely aware of his nephew's plans — asking him to put a stop to this, since the troops being raised come from Norwegian subjects. We send you, good Cornelius, and you, Voltemand, as bearers of this message to old Norway, giving you no authority beyond what these detailed documents allow. Farewell, and let your speed show your loyalty. CORNELIUS and VOLTEMAND. In that and all things, we will show our duty.
KING. We have no doubt of it. A hearty farewell.
[Exeunt Voltemand and Cornelius.]

KING. And now, Laertes, what's your news? You mentioned some request. What is it, Laertes? You can't make a reasonable request to the King of Denmark and have it refused. What would you ask, Laertes, that I wouldn't offer before you even asked? The head is no closer to the heart, the hand no more useful to the mouth, than Denmark's throne is to your father. What would you like, Laertes?

LAERTES. My lord, I ask your permission and blessing to return to France. Though I came willingly to Denmark to pay my respects at your coronation, I must confess that now my duty is done, my thoughts and wishes turn back toward France, and I humbly ask your gracious leave to go.
KING. Do you have your father's permission? What does Polonius say?
POLONIUS. He has, my lord. He wore me down with persistent asking, and I finally gave my reluctant consent. I beg you to let him go.
KING. Take your time, Laertes — it's yours. Use your best abilities however you wish. But now, my nephew Hamlet, and my son —
HAMLET. [Aside.] A little more than a relative, and a little less than kind.
KING. How is it that these clouds still hang over you?
HAMLET. Not at all, my lord. I'm too much in the sun.

QUEEN. Dear Hamlet, put off this dark mood, and look on the King of Denmark as a friend. Don't keep looking down with lowered eyes, searching for your noble father in the dust. You know it's the way of things — everything that lives must die, passing through nature into eternity.
HAMLET. Yes, madam, that is how things are.
QUEEN. If that's true, why does it seem to affect you so deeply?

HAMLET. Seem, madam? No — it is. I don't know anything about 'seeming.' It's not just my black cloak, good mother, or the usual dark clothes of mourning, or the heavy sighs I force myself to take, or the tears flowing from my eyes, or the sorrowful look on my face — together with all the outward forms and shows of grief — that can truly express what I feel. These things do only seem, because they're actions anyone could perform. But I have something inside me that goes beyond any outward show. These are just the costumes and trappings of grief.

KING. It's sweet and honorable of you, Hamlet, to pay these mourning duties to your father. But you must know that your father lost a father, and that father lost his, and each surviving son was bound by duty to grieve for a time. But to keep on with this stubborn mourning is a show of defiance toward heaven. It's unmanly grief; it reveals a weak heart, an impatient mind, and a simple understanding. Since what must be is as common as anything we experience, why should we stubbornly resist it? It's a fault against heaven, a fault against the dead, a fault against nature, and completely absurd — since the most universal truth is that fathers die, and every generation from the first has cried, 'This must be so.' We ask you to put aside this useless grief and think of us as a father. Let the world know: you are next in line for our throne, and we care for you with no less love than a devoted father has for his son. As for your plan to go back to school in Wittenberg, that's the opposite of what we want. We ask you to stay here in the comfort and warmth of our presence — our chief courtier, our nephew, and our son.
QUEEN. Don't refuse your mother's prayers, Hamlet. Please stay with us. Don't go to Wittenberg.
HAMLET. I'll do my best to obey you, madam.

KING. That's a loving and proper answer. Consider yourself at home here in Denmark. Madam, come — this gentle and willing agreement from Hamlet warms my heart. In honor of it, every toast the King of Denmark drinks today shall be announced with cannon fire, and the heavens themselves shall echo the thunder. Come, let's go.
[Exeunt all but Hamlet.]

HAMLET. Oh, if only this too-solid body would just melt, dissolve, and turn into dew! Or if God hadn't forbidden suicide. Oh God! Oh God! How exhausting, stale, flat, and pointless everything in this world seems to me! What a disgusting place — like a garden no one tends, overrun with weeds. Things rank and gross in nature have completely taken over. That it should come to this! Dead only two months — no, not even two. Such an excellent king, who was to this one as a sun god is to a goat. So loving to my mother that he wouldn't let the wind blow too roughly on her face. Heaven and earth — do I have to remember? She would hang on him as if her appetite grew by feeding on him. And yet, within a month — don't let me think about it. Frailty, thy name is woman! A mere month — before the shoes were even old that she wore following my poor father's coffin, crying like Niobe. And she — even she — oh God! A mindless animal would have mourned longer — married my uncle, my father's brother, who is no more like my father than I am like Hercules. Within a month — before the salt of her shameful tears had even dried in her reddened eyes — she married. Oh, what wicked haste, to rush so eagerly to an incestuous bed! This is not good, and it cannot lead to anything good. But break, my heart — I must keep silent.
[Enter Horatio, Marcellus and Barnardo]
HORATIO. Greetings, my lord!
HAMLET. I'm glad to see you well — Horatio, unless I'm mistaken.
HORATIO. The same, my lord, and your humble servant, as always.
HAMLET. Sir, my good friend — let me call you that instead. What brings you from Wittenberg, Horatio? Marcellus?
MARCELLUS. My lord.
HAMLET. I'm very glad to see you. Good evening, sir. But seriously, what brings you from Wittenberg?
HORATIO. A desire to play truant, my lord.

HAMLET. I wouldn't let your enemy say that about you, and I won't let you say it either. I know you're no truant. But what's your business in Elsinore? We'll teach you to drink heavily before you leave.
HORATIO. My lord, I came for your father's funeral.
HAMLET. Please don't mock me, fellow student. I think it was for my mother's wedding.
HORATIO. It did follow closely after, my lord.

HAMLET. Thrift, thrift, Horatio! The leftovers from the funeral were served cold at the wedding feast. I'd rather have met my worst enemy in heaven than have lived to see that day, Horatio. My father — I feel like I can see my father.
HORATIO. Where, my lord?
HAMLET. In my mind's eye, Horatio.
HORATIO. I saw him once. He was a great king.
HAMLET. He was a man — take him all in all. I will never see his like again.
HORATIO. My lord, I think I saw him last night.
HAMLET. Saw? Who?
HORATIO. My lord — the King, your father.
HAMLET. The King, my father!
HORATIO. Control your amazement for a moment and listen carefully while I tell you about this extraordinary event, with these gentlemen as witnesses.
HAMLET. For God's sake, let me hear it.

HORATIO. Two nights in a row, these gentlemen — Marcellus and Barnardo — while on their watch in the dead of night, had this encounter. A figure exactly like your father, fully armed from head to toe, appeared before them and walked slowly and majestically past them three times, staying within the length of a staff, while they — practically turned to jelly with fear — stood dumb and speechless. They told me about this in the strictest secrecy. I kept watch with them the third night, and exactly as they had described — the same time, the same form, every detail proven true — the ghost appeared. I knew your father. These two hands look no more alike.
HAMLET. But where was this?
MARCELLUS. My lord, on the platform where we keep watch.
HAMLET. Did you speak to it?

HORATIO. My lord, I did, but it gave no answer. Yet at one point I thought it lifted its head and seemed about to speak. But just then the morning rooster crowed loudly, and at the sound it shrank away and vanished from our sight.
HAMLET. That's very strange.
HORATIO. As sure as I'm alive, my lord, it's true. We felt it was our duty to tell you about it.
HAMLET. Yes, yes, absolutely, sirs — but this troubles me. Are you on watch tonight? MARCELLUS and BARNARDO. We are, my lord.
HAMLET. You say it was armed? Both. Armed, my lord.
HAMLET. From head to toe?
BOTH. From head to foot, my lord.
HAMLET. Then you didn't see his face?
HORATIO. Oh yes, my lord — his visor was up.
HAMLET. Did he look angry?
HORATIO. His expression showed more sorrow than anger.
HAMLET. Pale or flushed?
HORATIO. Very pale.
HAMLET. And did he keep his eyes fixed on you?
HORATIO. Without wavering.
HAMLET. I wish I had been there.
HORATIO. It would have amazed you.
HAMLET. I'm sure it would. Did it stay long?
HORATIO. About as long as it takes to count to a hundred at a moderate pace. MARCELLUS and BARNARDO. Longer, longer.
HORATIO. Not when I saw it.
HAMLET. His beard was grey, wasn't it?
HORATIO. It was, as I'd seen it in life — dark streaked with silver.
HAMLET. I'll keep watch tonight. Maybe it will walk again.
HORATIO. I'm sure it will.

HAMLET. If it takes on my noble father's form, I'll speak to it, even if hell itself opens wide and tells me to be silent. I ask all of you: if you've kept this secret until now, continue to keep it. And whatever else happens tonight, try to understand it but don't speak of it. I'll repay your loyalty. So farewell. I'll come to the platform between eleven and midnight to see you.
ALL. Our duty to your honor.
HAMLET. Your friendship, as mine is to you. Farewell.
[Exeunt Horatio, Marcellus and Barnardo.]

HAMLET. My father's ghost, in armor! Something is very wrong. I suspect foul play. I wish night would come! Until then, be still, my soul. Foul deeds will rise to the surface, no matter how deeply they're buried.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 3 — A Room in Polonius's House
paragraphs: [Enter Laertes and Ophelia]
LAERTES. My bags are packed and on the ship. Goodbye. And sister, whenever the winds are favorable and ships are available, don't forget to write to me.
OPHELIA. Do you doubt I would?

LAERTES. As for Hamlet and his attention to you — treat it as nothing more than a passing fancy, a youthful impulse. Think of it as a violet in spring — beautiful but not lasting. Sweet, but only for a moment. Nothing more.
OPHELIA. Nothing more than that?

LAERTES. Don't think of it as more. A young man doesn't just grow physically — as the body develops, so do the mind and soul. Perhaps he loves you now, and right now no dishonesty taints his intentions. But you have to understand — given his position, his will is not his own. He's bound by his birth. He can't just choose for himself the way ordinary people do, because the health and security of the whole state depends on his choices. So when he says he loves you, you'd be wise to believe it only as far as someone in his position can actually follow through — and that goes no further than what Denmark itself allows. Think about what you could lose if you listen too eagerly to his sweet talk, or give your heart away, or surrender your chastity to his reckless pursuit. Be careful, Ophelia — my dear sister. Stay back, out of the firing range of desire. Even the most careful young woman risks too much if she reveals her beauty to the world. Virtue itself can't escape vicious gossip. The worm destroys the bud in spring before it even opens, and in the fresh dew of youth, disease is most dangerous. Be cautious — safety lies in being careful. Youth rebels against itself, even without outside temptation.

OPHELIA. I'll take this good advice to heart. But dear brother, don't be like those hypocritical preachers who show me the steep and thorny road to heaven while they themselves walk the easy path of pleasure, ignoring their own advice.
LAERTES. Don't worry about me. I've stayed too long already. But here comes my father.
[Enter Polonius]
LAERTES. A second farewell is a double blessing — fortune smiles on a second leave-taking.
POLONIUS. You're still here, Laertes? Get on board, for shame! The wind is filling your sails, and they're waiting for you. Here — take my blessing.
[Laying his hand on Laertes's head.]

POLONIUS. And remember these few rules. Keep your thoughts to yourself, and don't act on any rash impulse. Be friendly, but not common. Hold tight to the friends you've tested and found true — bind them to your soul with hoops of steel. But don't waste your time on every new acquaintance you meet. Stay out of fights, but if you're in one, make sure your opponent fears you. Listen to everyone, but confide in few. Consider everyone's opinion, but reserve your own judgment. Dress as well as you can afford, but don't be flashy — expensive, not gaudy. Clothes often reveal the man, and in France, the best people dress with taste and distinction. Neither borrow nor lend money — lending often loses both the money and the friend, and borrowing dulls the edge of good management. Above all: be true to yourself. And it must follow, as night follows day, that you cannot then be false to anyone. Farewell — may my blessing make this wisdom take root in you.
LAERTES. I take my leave most humbly, my lord.
POLONIUS. It's time — go. Your servants are waiting.
LAERTES. Farewell, Ophelia. And remember what I told you.
OPHELIA. It's locked away in my memory, and you hold the key.
LAERTES. Farewell.
[Exit.]
POLONIUS. What did he say to you, Ophelia?
OPHELIA. Something about Lord Hamlet, if you please.

POLONIUS. Well remembered. I've been told that he's been spending a lot of private time with you lately, and that you've been very generous in granting him your company. If that's true — and I've been warned about it as a matter of concern — I have to tell you that you don't understand yourself as clearly as a daughter of mine should. What's going on between you? Tell me the truth.
OPHELIA. He has, my lord, recently made many declarations of his affection for me.
POLONIUS. Affection! Nonsense! You talk like a naive girl who hasn't been tested by such dangerous situations. Do you believe these declarations, as you call them?
OPHELIA. I don't know, my lord, what I should think.

POLONIUS. Well, I'll teach you. Think of yourself as a child who has mistaken counterfeit coins for real currency. Value yourself more highly, or — not to wear out the metaphor — you'll make a fool of me.
OPHELIA. My lord, he has pursued me with love in an honorable way.
POLONIUS. Honorable? Ha! That's one word for it.
OPHELIA. And he has backed up his words, my lord, with nearly every sacred vow of heaven.

POLONIUS. Those are just traps to catch the unwary. I know that when the blood runs hot, the soul recklessly makes promises. These flashes, daughter — giving more light than heat, burning out even as they're being made — you must not mistake for genuine fire. From now on, be less available. Set a higher price on your time than to come running whenever he asks. As for Lord Hamlet, believe this much about him: he is young, and he has a longer leash than you do. In short, Ophelia, don't believe his promises. They're go-betweens — not what they appear to be — mere promoters of dishonorable intentions, dressed up to sound pious and holy in order to deceive you. This is my final word: from this point forward, I do not want you wasting any of your free time talking with Lord Hamlet. See to it. Come along.
OPHELIA. I will obey, my lord.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 4 — The Platform
paragraphs: [Enter Hamlet, Horatio and Marcellus]
HAMLET. The air bites hard — it's very cold.
HORATIO. It's a sharp and bitter wind.
HAMLET. What time is it?
HORATIO. Not quite midnight, I think.
MARCELLUS. No, it's already struck.
HORATIO. Really? I didn't hear it. Then we're approaching the hour when the ghost usually appears.
[A flourish of trumpets, and ordnance shot off within.]
HORATIO. What does that mean, my lord?
HAMLET. The King is up drinking tonight, keeping the party going with noisy celebration. Every time he drains a glass of wine, the kettledrum and trumpet blast out a salute.
HORATIO. Is that a custom?

HAMLET. Yes, it is. And though I was born here and grew up with it, it's a custom I think is better broken than observed. This heavy drinking, known east and west, makes other nations call us drunkards and tarnish our reputation. And it does take the substance away from our real achievements, no matter how great they are. The same thing often happens with individual people — when they have some natural flaw they were born with, through no fault of their own, or some excessive tendency that overwhelms their reason, or some habit that corrupts their manners — these men, carrying the mark of a single defect, whether given by nature or by fortune, no matter how virtuous they are otherwise — as pure as grace itself, as capable as any person can be — will be condemned by public opinion because of that one particular fault. A drop of evil can ruin the noblest character.
HORATIO. Look, my lord — it's coming!
[Enter Ghost]

HAMLET. Angels and ministers of grace, defend us! Whether you are a good spirit or a demon, whether you bring air from heaven or fire from hell, whether your intentions are wicked or kind — you come in such a familiar shape that I will speak to you. I'll call you Hamlet, King, father, royal Dane. Answer me! Don't let me die in ignorance. Tell me — why have your sacred bones, sealed in death, burst from their burial wrappings? Why has the tomb where we saw you laid to rest opened its heavy marble jaws to throw you back among us? What does it mean that you, a dead body, dressed again in full armor, revisit the moonlit world, making the night terrible and shaking us so deeply with thoughts beyond our understanding? Tell me — why? What should we do?
[Ghost beckons Hamlet.]
HORATIO. It's beckoning you to follow it, as if it has something to tell you alone.
MARCELLUS. Look how gracefully it waves you toward a more isolated spot. But don't go with it.
HORATIO. Absolutely not.
HAMLET. It won't speak, so I'll follow it.
HORATIO. Don't, my lord!

HAMLET. Why not? What is there to fear? I don't value my life at a penny's worth. And as for my soul — what can it do to that? My soul is as immortal as the ghost itself. It's waving me forward again. I'll follow it.

HORATIO. What if it leads you toward the sea, my lord, or to the top of that terrifying cliff that juts out over the waves, and then takes on some other horrible shape that drives you out of your mind? Think about it. The place itself fills people with desperate thoughts, even without any other reason, just from looking down so far to the roaring sea below.
HAMLET. It's still waving. Go on, I'll follow you.
MARCELLUS. You can't go, my lord.
HAMLET. Take your hands off me.
HORATIO. Listen to reason — you can't go.
HAMLET. My destiny is calling, and every vein in my body is as strong as a lion's sinew.
[Ghost beckons.]
HAMLET. It's still calling. Let go of me, gentlemen.
[Breaking free from them.]
HAMLET. By heaven, I'll make a ghost of anyone who tries to stop me! Stand back! — Go on, I'll follow you.
[Exeunt Ghost and Hamlet.]
HORATIO. His imagination is making him reckless.
MARCELLUS. Let's follow him. We shouldn't just let him go.
HORATIO. Yes, let's go after him. Where will this lead?
MARCELLUS. Something is rotten in the state of Denmark.
HORATIO. Heaven will sort it out.
MARCELLUS. No — let's follow him.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 5 — A More Remote Part of the Castle
paragraphs: [Enter Ghost and Hamlet]
HAMLET. Where are you taking me? Speak — I'll go no further.
GHOST. Listen to me.
HAMLET. I will.
GHOST. My time is almost up. Soon I must return to the tormenting fires of purgatory.
HAMLET. Oh, you poor ghost!
GHOST. Don't pity me. Just listen carefully to what I'm about to tell you.
HAMLET. Speak. I'm bound to listen.
GHOST. And bound to take revenge, when you hear what I have to say.
HAMLET. What?

GHOST. I am your father's spirit, condemned for a time to walk the earth at night and burn in fires by day, until the sins of my mortal life are purged away. If I weren't forbidden to reveal the secrets of my prison, I could tell you a story whose mildest word would freeze your blood, make your eyes bulge from their sockets, and make every hair on your head stand on end like the quills of a porcupine. But these eternal mysteries are not for mortal ears. Listen — listen! If you ever loved your father —
HAMLET. Oh God!
GHOST. Avenge his foul and most unnatural murder.
HAMLET. Murder!
GHOST. Murder most foul — as all murder is — but this was the foulest, strangest, and most unnatural.
HAMLET. Tell me quickly, so I can fly to my revenge as fast as thought itself or the wings of love.

GHOST. I see you're ready. You'd have to be duller than the lazy weed rotting on the banks of the river of forgetfulness to not be stirred by this. Now listen, Hamlet. The official story is that a serpent stung me while I slept in my orchard. All of Denmark has been grossly deceived by this false account of my death. But know this, noble young man: the serpent that stung your father now wears his crown.
HAMLET. Oh, my prophetic soul! My uncle!

GHOST. Yes, that incestuous, adulterous beast. With the witchcraft of his cleverness and his treacherous charm — oh, wicked wit and gifts that have the power to seduce! — he won over the desires of my seemingly virtuous queen. Oh Hamlet, what a collapse that was! From me, whose love was so devoted that it matched every vow I made to her in marriage, to decline to a wretch whose natural abilities were so inferior to mine. But just as virtue can never be corrupted, even when lust courts it in the form of an angel, so lust — even when linked to a shining angel — will eventually grow tired of a heavenly partner and feed on garbage. But wait — I think I sense the morning air. Let me be brief. While I was sleeping in my orchard, as I always did in the afternoon, your uncle crept up on me with a vial of poisonous liquid and poured it into my ears. The poison works so violently against human blood that it races through the body like quicksilver, curdling the blood like acid dropped into milk. That's what it did to me — and instantly, a horrible crust covered my entire body, like a leper's skin. So I was robbed — while sleeping, by my own brother's hand — of my life, my crown, and my queen, all at once. Cut off in the fullness of my sins, without confession, without communion, without last rites — sent to face my judgment with all my imperfections still on my head. Oh horrible! Oh horrible! Most horrible! If you have any natural feeling, don't let this stand. Don't let the royal bed of Denmark become a couch for lust and damned incest. But however you pursue this act, don't let your mind be corrupted, and don't plot anything against your mother. Leave her to heaven and to the thorns of guilt that will prick and sting her conscience. Farewell now! The glowworm shows that morning is near and begins to fade its pale light. Goodbye, goodbye, goodbye. Remember me.
[Exit.]

HAMLET. Oh, all you powers of heaven! Oh earth! What else? Should I call on hell too? No! Hold together, my heart. And you, my body, don't suddenly grow weak — hold me up. Remember you? Yes, you poor ghost, as long as memory exists in this troubled mind. Remember you? Yes — I'll wipe away from my memory every trivial record, every lesson from books, every impression that youth and experience have written there. Your command alone shall live in the pages of my brain, unmixed with lesser things. Yes, by heaven! Oh, most treacherous woman! Oh villain, villain, smiling damned villain! Let me write this down — that a man may smile and smile and still be a villain. At least I'm sure that's true in Denmark.
[Writing.]
HAMLET. So, uncle, there you are. Now, my promise: 'Goodbye, goodbye, remember me.' I have sworn it. HORATIO and MARCELLUS. [Within.] My lord! My lord!
MARCELLUS. [Within.] Lord Hamlet!
HORATIO. [Within.] Heaven protect him!
HAMLET. So be it!
MARCELLUS. [Within.] Hello there, my lord!
HAMLET. Hello! Come, bird, come!
[Enter Horatio and Marcellus]
MARCELLUS. How are you, my noble lord?
HORATIO. What news, my lord?
HAMLET. Oh, incredible news!
HORATIO. Good my lord, tell us.
HAMLET. No — you'd reveal it.
HORATIO. Not I, my lord, I swear it.
MARCELLUS. Nor I, my lord.
HAMLET. What would you say — would any man believe it? But will you keep it secret? HORATIO and MARCELLUS. Yes, by heaven, my lord.
HAMLET. There's not a villain in all Denmark who isn't a complete scoundrel.
HORATIO. We don't need a ghost rising from the grave to tell us that, my lord.

HAMLET. You're right, you're absolutely right. And so, without any further discussion, I think it's best that we shake hands and go our separate ways — you back to whatever business you have, since every man has his business — and as for me, I think I'll go pray.
HORATIO. These are wild and rambling words, my lord.
HAMLET. I'm sorry they offend you — truly, sincerely sorry.
HORATIO. There's no offense, my lord.

HAMLET. Oh yes there is, Horatio — by Saint Patrick, there is. And great offense too. As for what we saw tonight — it is an honest ghost, let me tell you that. As for what passed between us, contain your curiosity as best you can. And now, good friends, as you are my friends, scholars, and soldiers, grant me one small request.
HORATIO. What is it, my lord? We will.
HAMLET. Never tell anyone what you've seen tonight. HORATIO and MARCELLUS. We won't, my lord.
HAMLET. No, swear it.
HORATIO. I swear, my lord.
MARCELLUS. I swear, my lord.
HAMLET. Swear on my sword.
MARCELLUS. We've already sworn, my lord.
HAMLET. I mean it — swear on my sword.
GHOST. [Cries under the stage.] Swear.
HAMLET. Ha! You hear that, do you? Are you there, old friend? Come on — you can hear this fellow down in the basement. Agree to swear.
HORATIO. Tell us the oath, my lord.
HAMLET. Never to speak of what you've seen. Swear on my sword.
GHOST. [Beneath.] Swear.
HAMLET. Here and everywhere? Then we'll change our position. Come here, gentlemen, and put your hands on my sword again. Never to speak of what you've heard. Swear on my sword.
GHOST. [Beneath.] Swear.
HAMLET. Well done, old mole! You can burrow through the earth fast! A fine digger! Let's move again, friends.
HORATIO. Good God, this is unbelievably strange.

HAMLET. Then welcome it as something strange. There are more things in heaven and earth, Horatio, than are dreamt of in your philosophy. But come — here, as before, never — so help you God — no matter how strange or oddly I may behave from now on — as I may find it necessary to put on a show of madness — you must never, at such times, fold your arms like this, or shake your head, or say something vague like 'Well, we know,' or 'We could say something if we wanted to,' or 'If we chose to speak,' or 'There are people who could tell you' — or any other hint that you know anything about me. This you must not do. So help you God's grace and mercy, swear.
GHOST. [Beneath.] Swear.

HAMLET. Rest, rest, troubled spirit. So, gentlemen, with all my love I entrust myself to you. And whatever poor Hamlet can do to show his love and friendship to you, God willing, he will do. Let's go in together, and remember — keep your fingers on your lips. The world has gone wrong. Oh, what a cursed fate, that I was ever born to set it right! No — come, let's go together.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 1 — A Room in Polonius's House
paragraphs: [Enter Polonius and Reynaldo]
POLONIUS. Give him this money and these letters, Reynaldo.
REYNALDO. I will, my lord.
POLONIUS. You'd be very wise, good Reynaldo, to ask around about his behavior before you go see him.
REYNALDO. My lord, that was exactly my plan.

POLONIUS. Good, very good. Look, sir — first find out which Danes are in Paris, how they live, who they associate with, where they stay, what they spend, and what company they keep. By circling around the topic with indirect questions, if you find that they know my son, you'll learn more than by asking directly. Pretend you have a distant acquaintance with him — like, 'I know his father and his friends, and I sort of know him.' Do you follow me, Reynaldo?
REYNALDO. Yes, very well, my lord.

POLONIUS. 'And I sort of know him, but,' you might say, 'not well. But if he's the one I mean, he's pretty wild — addicted to this and that.' Pin whatever stories you want on him — nothing so bad as to disgrace him, mind you — but the kind of casual, wild indiscretions that typically go hand in hand with youth and freedom.
REYNALDO. Like gambling, my lord?
POLONIUS. Sure — or drinking, fencing, swearing, fighting, visiting women. You can go that far.
REYNALDO. My lord, that would disgrace him.

POLONIUS. Not at all — if you present it the right way. Don't make him sound like a complete degenerate — that's not what I mean. Just hint at his faults delicately enough that they sound like the natural overflow of a spirited young man — a wildness in hot young blood that everyone experiences.
REYNALDO. But my lord —
POLONIUS. What's the point of all this, you want to know?
REYNALDO. Yes, my lord, I would.

POLONIUS. Here's my strategy, and I think it's a clever one. By casting these little aspersions on my son — making him sound slightly rough around the edges — the person you're talking to, if they've ever seen the young man guilty of the things you mention, will agree with you and say something like, 'Yes, sir,' or 'friend,' or 'gentleman' — depending on the person and their manner of speaking.
REYNALDO. Very good, my lord.
POLONIUS. And then, sir, he does this — he does — what was I about to say? Good grief, I was about to say something. Where did I leave off?
REYNALDO. At 'agrees with you,' at 'friend or so' and 'gentleman.'

POLONIUS. At 'agrees with you' — yes, exactly! He agrees with you like this: 'I know the gentleman. I saw him yesterday, or the day before, or then, with so-and-so. And, as you say, he was gambling, or I caught him drunk, or I saw him get into a fight at tennis,' or maybe, 'I saw him go into a certain house' — meaning a brothel. You see? Your bait of false accusations catches the fish of truth. And this is how wise, far-reaching people use indirect methods to find out the truth. That's my lesson and my advice — use it to check on my son. You understand?
REYNALDO. I do, my lord.
POLONIUS. God be with you. Farewell.
REYNALDO. Good day, my lord.
POLONIUS. Watch his tendencies for yourself.
REYNALDO. I will, my lord.
POLONIUS. And let him enjoy his music.
REYNALDO. Yes, my lord.
POLONIUS. Farewell.
[Exit Reynaldo.]
[Enter Ophelia]
POLONIUS. What's the matter, Ophelia?
OPHELIA. Oh my lord, I've been so frightened!
POLONIUS. By what, in God's name?

OPHELIA. My lord, I was sewing in my room when Lord Hamlet came in — his jacket all unfastened, no hat on his head, his stockings dirty and falling down to his ankles, pale as his shirt, his knees knocking together, and with a look on his face so full of misery that he seemed to have escaped from hell itself to tell of horrors. He came right up to me.
POLONIUS. Mad with love for you?
OPHELIA. My lord, I don't know, but I truly fear it.
POLONIUS. What did he say?

OPHELIA. He grabbed my wrist and held me tight. Then he stretched his arm out full length and, with his other hand over his brow, studied my face as if he were trying to draw it. He stood like that for a long time. Finally, with a little shake of my arm and three slow nods of his head, he let out a sigh so deep and pitiful it seemed to shatter his whole body. Then he let me go. He turned his head to look back at me over his shoulder and seemed to find his way out without using his eyes, because he kept them fixed on me until the very end.

POLONIUS. Come with me — I'm going to see the King. This is the madness of love, a violent passion that destroys itself and drives the will to desperate acts. I'm sorry — have you been harsh with him lately?
OPHELIA. No, my lord. But as you instructed, I refused his letters and denied him access to me.

POLONIUS. That's what drove him mad. I'm sorry I didn't judge the situation better. I was afraid he was just playing with you and meant to ruin you. But curse my suspicion! It seems that as we get older, we tend to overthink things, just as young people tend to be rash. Come, let's go to the King. This must be made known — keeping it secret could cause more harm than revealing it.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 2 — A Room in the Castle
paragraphs: [Enter King, Queen, Rosencrantz, Guildenstern and Attendants]

KING. Welcome, dear Rosencrantz and Guildenstern. Beyond our great desire to see you, the need to use your help prompted us to send for you so urgently. You've heard something about Hamlet's transformation — I call it that, since neither his outer manner nor his inner self resembles what it was. What could have put him so far out of sorts, other than his father's death, I can't imagine. I ask you both — since you grew up with him and are so familiar with his personality and habits — to spend some time here at our court and draw him toward enjoyable activities, while gathering whatever information you can about whether something we don't know about is troubling him, so that we might be able to help.

QUEEN. Good gentlemen, he's talked about you often, and I'm sure there's no one alive he's more attached to. If you'd be kind enough to spend some time with us, your visit will receive the kind of thanks that befits a king's gratitude.
ROSENCRANTZ. Both your Majesties have such power over us that you could simply command rather than request.
GUILDENSTERN. We both obey. We're completely at your service, ready to be commanded.
KING. Thanks, Rosencrantz and kind Guildenstern.
QUEEN. Thanks, Guildenstern and kind Rosencrantz. I beg you to visit my much-changed son right away. Someone go and bring these gentlemen to where Hamlet is.
GUILDENSTERN. May heaven make our presence helpful to him.
QUEEN. Amen to that.
[Exeunt Rosencrantz, Guildenstern and some Attendants.]
[Enter Polonius]
POLONIUS. The ambassadors from Norway, my lord, have returned with good news.
KING. You've always been a bearer of good news.

POLONIUS. Have I, my lord? I assure you, I hold my duty as sacred as my soul, both to God and to my gracious King. And I believe — unless my mind has lost its skill at following political matters — that I have found the real cause of Hamlet's madness.
KING. Tell me — I'm eager to hear.
POLONIUS. Let's first receive the ambassadors. My news will be the dessert to that feast.
KING. Go welcome them yourself and bring them in.
[Exit Polonius.]
KING. He tells me, my dear queen, that he's found the source of your son's troubles.
QUEEN. I suspect it's nothing more than the obvious — his father's death and our hasty marriage.
KING. Well, we'll get to the bottom of it.
[Enter Polonius with Voltemand and Cornelius]
KING. Welcome, my good friends! What news from our brother Norway, Voltemand?

VOLTEMAND. He sends his warmest greetings and regards. When we first raised the issue, he sent out to suppress his nephew's military buildup, which he initially thought was directed against Poland. But upon closer investigation, he discovered it was aimed at your Majesty. Distressed that his illness, age, and weakness had been taken advantage of, he had Fortinbras arrested. Fortinbras obeyed, received a rebuke from Norway, and finally swore before his uncle never to take up arms against your Majesty again. The old king, overjoyed, gave Fortinbras three thousand crowns a year and permission to use those same troops against Poland instead. He requests, as detailed here —
[Gives a paper.]
VOLTEMAND. — that you grant safe passage through your territory for this campaign, under the conditions specified in this document.
KING. Very good. We'll read it over carefully, respond, and make our decision. Meanwhile, thank you for your efforts. Get some rest — tonight we'll celebrate together. Most welcome home.
[Exeunt Voltemand and Cornelius.]

POLONIUS. That business is settled nicely. Now, my lord and madam — to waste time explaining what majesty is, what duty is, why day is day and night is night, would be nothing but a waste of time. Therefore, since brevity is the soul of wit, and long-windedness is mere decoration, I'll be brief: your noble son is mad. Mad, I call it, because what is true madness but being completely mad? But enough of that.
QUEEN. More substance and less style, please.

POLONIUS. Madam, I swear I'm using no style at all. That he is mad is true. It's true and it's a pity. And it's a pity it's true — that's a silly way to put it, but forget the clever phrasing, because I'm not trying to be clever. Let's agree he's mad, then. Now the question is: what's causing it? Because this faulty effect has a cause. Here's what remains. Consider this: I have a daughter — mine while she's mine — who, out of duty and obedience, has given me this. Now listen and draw your conclusions.
[Reads.]
POLONIUS. 'To the heavenly and idol of my soul, the most beautified Ophelia' — That's a terrible phrase, a vulgar phrase. 'Beautified' is a vulgar word. But listen to the rest.
[Reads.]
POLONIUS. 'In her excellent white bosom, these,' etcetera.
QUEEN. Did this come from Hamlet?
POLONIUS. Good madam, wait — I'll read it faithfully.
[Reads.]

POLONIUS. 'Doubt that the stars are fire, Doubt that the sun moves, Doubt that truth itself is a liar, But never doubt that I love. Oh dear Ophelia, I'm bad at writing poetry. I don't have the skill to express my feelings in verse. But believe that I love you best — oh, the very best, believe it. Goodbye. Yours forever, most dear lady, as long as this body is his to give, HAMLET.' My daughter showed me this out of obedience. And beyond this, she's told me about all his romantic approaches — when, how, and where they happened.
KING. But how has she responded to his love?
POLONIUS. What do you think of me?
KING. As a faithful and honorable man.

POLONIUS. I'd like to prove that I am. But what would you think if, when I first noticed this burning love — and I noticed it, I must tell you, before my daughter told me — what would you or the Queen here think if I had just ignored it, or looked the other way, or stayed silent? What would you think? No — I went straight to work and told my young lady: 'Lord Hamlet is a prince, far above your reach. This cannot happen.' And I ordered her to refuse his company, reject his messages, and accept no gifts. She obeyed, and he — rejected — fell into sadness, then stopped eating, then couldn't sleep, then grew weak, then delirious, and finally into the madness that now has him raving — which is what we're all so worried about.
KING. Do you think that's what it is?
QUEEN. It's very possible.
POLONIUS. Has there ever been a time — I'd like to know — when I said 'It's definitely this' and I turned out to be wrong?
KING. Not that I know of.
POLONIUS. I'll stake my head on it.
[Points to his head and shoulder.]
POLONIUS. If the evidence leads me, I'll find where the truth is hiding, even if it's buried deep.
KING. How can we test this further?
POLONIUS. You know he sometimes walks in this hallway for hours at a time.
QUEEN. He certainly does.

POLONIUS. At one of those times, I'll send my daughter to him. You and I will hide behind a curtain and observe the encounter. If he doesn't love her, and that's not what's driving him mad, then I'll give up my position and go tend a farm.
KING. We'll try it.
[Enter Hamlet, reading]
QUEEN. But look — there comes the poor man, reading by himself and looking miserable.
POLONIUS. Please, both of you — leave us. I'll approach him right now. Give me a moment.
[Exeunt King, Queen and Attendants.]
POLONIUS. How are you doing, my good Lord Hamlet?
HAMLET. Well, thank God.
POLONIUS. Do you know who I am, my lord?
HAMLET. Very well. You're a fishmonger.
POLONIUS. Not I, my lord.
HAMLET. Then I wish you were that honest.
POLONIUS. Honest, my lord?
HAMLET. Yes, sir. To be honest, in this world, is to be one man picked out of ten thousand.
POLONIUS. That's very true, my lord.
HAMLET. Because if the sun can breed maggots in a dead dog — do you have a daughter?
POLONIUS. I do, my lord.
HAMLET. Don't let her walk in the sun. Conception is a blessing, but not the kind your daughter might conceive. Keep an eye on her, friend.

POLONIUS. What do you mean by that? [Aside.] Still going on about my daughter. Yet he didn't recognize me at first — he called me a fishmonger. He's far gone, far gone. And honestly, in my youth I suffered terribly from love too — nearly this bad. I'll try again. — What are you reading, my lord?
HAMLET. Words, words, words.
POLONIUS. What's it about, my lord?
HAMLET. Between whom?
POLONIUS. I mean what's the subject matter you're reading, my lord.

HAMLET. Slander, sir. This satirical writer claims that old men have grey beards, wrinkled faces, eyes oozing thick goo, and a severe lack of intelligence, along with very weak legs. All of which, sir, I believe with absolute conviction, yet I think it's rude to put it in print. Because you yourself, sir, would be as old as I am if, like a crab, you could walk backwards.
POLONIUS. [Aside.] Though this is madness, there's a method to it. — Would you like to step out of this drafty hallway, my lord?
HAMLET. Into my grave?

POLONIUS. Indeed, that would be out of the draft. [Aside.] How sharp his replies are sometimes! That's a kind of insight that madness often stumbles onto, which sanity couldn't produce so neatly. I'll leave him now and immediately arrange a meeting between him and my daughter. — My lord, I'll take my humble leave of you.
HAMLET. You can't take anything from me that I'd more willingly part with — except my life, except my life, except my life.
POLONIUS. Farewell, my lord.
HAMLET. These tedious old fools.
[Enter Rosencrantz and Guildenstern]
POLONIUS. You're looking for Lord Hamlet — there he is.
ROSENCRANTZ. [To Polonius.] God save you, sir.
[Exit Polonius.]
GUILDENSTERN. My honored lord!
ROSENCRANTZ. My dear lord!
HAMLET. My excellent friends! How are you, Guildenstern? And Rosencrantz! Good fellows, how are you both?
ROSENCRANTZ. Like ordinary people, getting by.
GUILDENSTERN. Happy enough — not too happy. We're not at the top of Fortune's wheel.
HAMLET. Nor at the bottom of her shoe?
ROSENCRANTZ. Neither, my lord.
HAMLET. Then you're somewhere around her waist, or in the middle of her favors?
GUILDENSTERN. We're her private servants, you might say.
HAMLET. In Fortune's most private parts? Oh yes, she is a fickle mistress. What's the news?
ROSENCRANTZ. None, my lord, except that the world has become honest.
HAMLET. Then doomsday must be near. But your news isn't true. Let me ask more specifically: what have you done to deserve Fortune sending you to this prison?
GUILDENSTERN. Prison, my lord?
HAMLET. Denmark's a prison.
ROSENCRANTZ. Then the whole world is one.
HAMLET. A big one, with many cells, wards, and dungeons — Denmark being one of the worst.
ROSENCRANTZ. We don't think so, my lord.
HAMLET. Well, then it isn't one to you. Nothing is either good or bad — it's thinking that makes it so. To me, it's a prison.
ROSENCRANTZ. Then your ambition makes it one. It's too small for your mind.
HAMLET. Oh God, I could be shut up in a nutshell and count myself a king of infinite space — if it weren't for the bad dreams.
GUILDENSTERN. Those dreams are really just ambition. The very substance of an ambitious person is nothing more than the shadow of a dream.
HAMLET. A dream itself is just a shadow.
ROSENCRANTZ. Exactly — and I think ambition is so light and insubstantial that it's just the shadow of a shadow.
HAMLET. Then beggars are the real solid beings, and monarchs and heroes are just beggars' shadows. Shall we go to court? I'm not reasoning very well. ROSENCRANTZ and GUILDENSTERN. We'll attend you.
HAMLET. No, not as servants. I won't rank you with my other attendants, because, to be honest, I'm very poorly served these days. But, as old friends — what brings you to Elsinore?
ROSENCRANTZ. To visit you, my lord. No other reason.

HAMLET. Poor as I am, I'm even poor in thanks — but I thank you. And I'm sure, dear friends, my thanks aren't worth much. Were you sent for? Is this your own idea? A free visit? Come, be honest with me. Come on — speak.
GUILDENSTERN. What should we say, my lord?
HAMLET. Anything — just tell the truth. You were sent for, and there's a kind of confession in your faces that you're not clever enough to hide. I know the King and Queen sent for you.
ROSENCRANTZ. For what purpose, my lord?

HAMLET. That's what you'll have to tell me. But let me appeal to you — by our friendship, by our shared youth, by the bond of love between us, and by anything more persuasive that a better speaker could invoke — be straight with me. Were you sent for or not?
ROSENCRANTZ. [To Guildenstern.] What do you say?
HAMLET. [Aside.] Ah, I've got your number. If you love me, don't hold back.
GUILDENSTERN. My lord, we were sent for.

HAMLET. I'll tell you why, so you won't have to reveal what the King and Queen told you. I have lately — though I don't know why — lost all my enjoyment, given up all my usual activities. Everything feels so heavy that this magnificent earth seems to me like a barren wasteland. This beautiful canopy of sky — this magnificent overhanging firmament, this majestic roof decorated with golden fire — it all looks like nothing more than a foul, pestilent collection of fumes. What a piece of work is man! How noble in reason, how infinite in ability! In form and movement, how precise and admirable! In action, like an angel! In understanding, like a god! The beauty of the world, the masterpiece of all living things. And yet, to me, what is this ultimate distillation of dust? Man gives me no delight — nor woman either, though your smiling suggests you think otherwise.
ROSENCRANTZ. My lord, I had no such thought.
HAMLET. Then why did you laugh when I said 'Man gives me no delight'?

ROSENCRANTZ. I was thinking, my lord, that if you have no delight in man, what a poor reception the actors will get from you. We passed them on the road — they're on their way here to perform for you.

HAMLET. The one who plays the king will be welcome — his Majesty will get tribute from me. The adventurous knight can use his sword and shield. The lover won't sigh for nothing. The comedian can finish his part in peace. The clown will make the easy laughers laugh. And the lady can speak her mind freely, or the rhythm will suffer. What company is it?
ROSENCRANTZ. The same ones you used to enjoy so much — the city tragedians.
HAMLET. How is it they're traveling? They did better in every way staying in the city.
ROSENCRANTZ. I think recent developments forced them out.
HAMLET. Are they still as well-regarded as when I was in the city? Do they still draw crowds?
ROSENCRANTZ. No, they don't.
HAMLET. How's that? Have they gotten rusty?

ROSENCRANTZ. No, they work as hard as ever. But there's a troupe of child actors — little hawks — who screech louder than anyone and get wildly applauded for it. They're the fashion now, and they've so ridiculed the regular theaters that many grown actors are afraid of being satirized and hardly dare perform anymore.

HAMLET. What — they're children? Who supports them? Who pays their bills? Will they only keep acting until their voices break? Won't they complain later, if they grow up to be regular actors — as is likely, if they have no other income — that their writers did them wrong by making them attack their own future profession?

ROSENCRANTZ. Actually, there's been a lot of controversy on both sides, and the public thinks it's great entertainment to egg them on. For a while, no one would invest in a play unless the playwright and the actors were fighting about it.
HAMLET. Is that possible?
GUILDENSTERN. Oh, there's been plenty of intellectual battling.
HAMLET. Do the boys win?
ROSENCRANTZ. They do, my lord — they've even taken on the biggest names.

HAMLET. That's not so strange, really. My uncle is King of Denmark, and people who used to mock him while my father was alive now pay forty or fifty ducats for a miniature portrait of him. There's something unnatural in all this, if philosophy could figure it out.
[Flourish of trumpets within.]
GUILDENSTERN. There are the players now.

HAMLET. Gentlemen, you're welcome to Elsinore. Let me shake your hands. The proper accompaniment to a welcome is courtesy and ceremony. Let me greet you formally, so that my welcome to the players — which I assure you will look very warm — doesn't seem warmer than my welcome to you. You're welcome. But my uncle-father and aunt-mother are mistaken.
GUILDENSTERN. Mistaken about what, my dear lord?
HAMLET. I'm only mad when the wind blows from the north-northwest. When the wind is from the south, I can tell a hawk from a handsaw.
[Enter Polonius]
POLONIUS. Greetings, gentlemen.
HAMLET. Listen, Guildenstern — and you too, lean in. That big baby you see there hasn't outgrown his swaddling clothes yet.
ROSENCRANTZ. Maybe he's wearing them for the second time — they say an old man is a child twice over.
HAMLET. I predict he's coming to tell me about the players. Watch. — You're right, sir — it certainly was so, on a Monday morning.
POLONIUS. My lord, I have news for you.
HAMLET. My lord, I have news for you. When Roscius was an actor in Rome —
POLONIUS. The actors have arrived, my lord.
HAMLET. Old news.
POLONIUS. On my honor —
HAMLET. Then came each actor on his donkey —

POLONIUS. They're the best actors in the world — for tragedy, comedy, history, pastoral, pastoral-comical, historical-pastoral, tragical-historical, tragical-comical-historical-pastoral, continuous drama, or anything without rules. No one can be too heavy or too light for them. They're the only company worth seeing.
HAMLET. Oh Jephthah, judge of Israel — what a treasure you had!
POLONIUS. What treasure, my lord?
HAMLET. Why — 'One fair daughter and no more, whom he loved very dearly.'
POLONIUS. [Aside.] Still going on about my daughter.
HAMLET. Am I not right, old Jephthah?
POLONIUS. If you call me Jephthah, my lord, I do have a daughter I love dearly.
HAMLET. No, that's not what follows.
POLONIUS. What follows, then, my lord?
HAMLET. Why — 'As fate would have it,' and then, you know, 'It came to pass, as was most likely.' The first verse of the old song will tell you more. But look — here comes my entertainment.
[Enter four or five Players]

HAMLET. Welcome, all of you! I'm glad to see you well. Welcome, good friends. Oh, my old friend! Your face has grown a beard since I saw you last — are you here to challenge me in Denmark? And my young lady! By heaven, your ladyship has grown taller since I last saw you — a good few inches closer to heaven. I hope your voice, like a coin, hasn't cracked out of circulation. Welcome, everyone. Let's get right to it, like eager falconers chasing anything that flies. Give us a speech right now — a passionate one.
FIRST PLAYER. What speech, my lord?

HAMLET. I once heard you deliver a speech that was never performed publicly — or if it was, only once, because the play didn't appeal to the masses. It was caviar to the general public. But it was — as I and others whose judgment I respect agreed — an excellent play, well-structured, written with skill and restraint. Someone said it had no crude jokes to spice things up and no pretentious language that would make the author seem affected, but called it an honest, well-crafted work — as wholesome as it was elegant, and much more substantial than flashy. There was one speech in it I especially loved — Aeneas's tale to Dido, particularly the part about Priam's slaughter. If you remember it, start from this line — let me think — 'The savage Pyrrhus, like the Hyrcanian beast' — no, that's not it. It starts with Pyrrhus. 'The savage Pyrrhus — he whose dark arms, black as his murderous purpose, matched the night when he lay hidden in the wooden horse — now has his dreadful, dark complexion smeared with even more terrible markings. From head to foot he is drenched in red, horribly splashed with the blood of fathers, mothers, daughters, and sons, baked and crusted by the burning streets that cast a tyrannical, hellish light on their vile murders. Roasted in fury and fire, coated with clotted gore, with eyes like burning coals, the hellish Pyrrhus seeks old Priam.' Go on from there.
POLONIUS. That was well spoken, my lord — good delivery and good feeling.

FIRST PLAYER. Soon he finds him, striking uselessly at Greeks. His ancient sword, too heavy for his old arm, falls where it lands, refusing to obey him. In an unequal fight, Pyrrhus drives at Priam, striking wide in his fury. But just the rush of wind from his terrible sword knocks the feeble old man down. Then the very walls of Troy seemed to feel this blow, and the flaming rooftop crashed down with a hideous noise, freezing Pyrrhus in his tracks. For look — his sword, which was about to fall on Priam's white-haired head, seemed to stick in the air. Like a painted figure, Pyrrhus stood motionless, suspended between his will and his action, doing nothing. But just as we often see before a storm — silence in the heavens, the clouds standing still, the wild winds speechless, the world below as quiet as death — and then suddenly the terrible thunder rips through the sky — so, after that pause, fresh vengeance drove Pyrrhus back to his work. And never did the giant Cyclops's hammers fall on the god of war's eternal armor with less mercy than Pyrrhus's bloody sword now fell on Priam. Down, down with you, fickle Fortune! All you gods, take away her power! Break the wheel she spins! And hurl it down from the heights of heaven to the depths of hell!
POLONIUS. This is too long.
HAMLET. It'll go to the barber's, along with your beard. — Please, continue. He's the type who only likes a dance number or a dirty joke, or he falls asleep. Go on — get to Hecuba.
FIRST PLAYER. 'But who — oh, who — had seen the grief-stricken queen —'
HAMLET. 'The grief-stricken queen'?
POLONIUS. That's good! 'Grief-stricken queen' is good.

FIRST PLAYER. Running barefoot through the streets, threatening the flames with blinding tears. A rag upon her head where the crown once sat, and for a robe, a blanket snatched up in panic around her exhausted body — anyone who had seen her, with a tongue dipped in venom, would have called Fortune a traitor. But if the gods themselves had seen her — when she saw Pyrrhus savagely hacking her husband's body to pieces — the shriek she let out, unless nothing mortal could move them, would have brought tears to the burning eyes of heaven and stirred passion in the gods.
POLONIUS. Look — he's gone pale and has tears in his eyes. No more, please.

HAMLET. Fine. I'll have you finish the rest soon. — Good my lord, will you see that the players are well taken care of? Treat them well — they are the mirrors and brief chronicles of the age. You'd rather have a bad epitaph after your death than their bad review while you're alive.
POLONIUS. My lord, I will treat them as they deserve.

HAMLET. Good God, man — much better than that! Treat every man as he deserves, and who would escape a whipping? Treat them according to your own honor and dignity. The less they deserve, the more credit your generosity earns. Take them in.
POLONIUS. Come, sirs.
HAMLET. Follow him, friends. We'll see a play tomorrow.
[Exeunt Polonius with all the Players but the First.]
HAMLET. Listen, old friend — can you perform The Murder of Gonzago?
FIRST PLAYER. Yes, my lord.
HAMLET. We'll have it tomorrow night. Could you, if needed, learn and insert a speech of about twelve to sixteen lines that I'll write for you?
FIRST PLAYER. Yes, my lord.
HAMLET. Very good. Follow that lord, and make sure you don't make fun of him.
[Exit First Player.]
HAMLET. [To Rosencrantz and Guildenstern] Good friends, I'll leave you until tonight. You're welcome to Elsinore.
ROSENCRANTZ. Thank you, my lord.
[Exeunt Rosencrantz and Guildenstern.]

HAMLET. Right then — goodbye. Now I'm alone. Oh, what a worthless, pathetic slave I am! Isn't it incredible that this actor, working with nothing but fiction — a fantasy of emotion — could force his soul into such sympathy with his role that his face went pale, tears came to his eyes, his voice broke, and his whole body shaped itself to match his feeling? And all for nothing! For Hecuba! What's Hecuba to him, or he to Hecuba, that he should weep for her? What would he do if he had the motive and the cause for passion that I have? He'd drown the stage in tears and shatter every ear with terrifying speech, drive the guilty mad, horrify the innocent, confuse the ignorant, and overwhelm the very powers of sight and hearing. Yet here I am — a dull, spiritless coward — moping around like a daydreamer, indifferent to my cause, unable to say a word. Not a word — for a king whose life and throne were stolen through damned treachery. Am I a coward? Who calls me a villain? Who slaps me across the face? Pulls my beard? Tweaks my nose? Calls me a liar to my face? Who does this to me? I should take it, because I must be coward-hearted, lacking the gall to fight back — otherwise I would have fed every vulture in the sky with this villain's guts by now. Bloody, lecherous, remorseless, treacherous, unnatural villain! Oh, revenge! But why am I ranting like this? This is pathetic — that I, the son of a murdered father, urged to revenge by heaven and hell itself, must pour out my heart with words like a prostitute and curse like a kitchen maid. Shame on me! Enough! Think, brain! I've heard that guilty people watching a play have sometimes been so struck by the scene that they've confessed their crimes on the spot. Because murder, though it has no tongue, will speak through the most miraculous means. I'll have these players perform something like my father's murder in front of my uncle. I'll watch his face. I'll probe him deeply. If he even flinches, I'll know what to do. The spirit I saw may be the devil — and the devil can disguise himself in a pleasing shape. Maybe, out of my weakness and depression — since he's very powerful with such vulnerable spirits — he's trying to trick me into damning myself. I need better proof than this. The play's the thing — I'll use it to catch the conscience of the King.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 1 — A Room in the Castle
paragraphs: [Enter King, Queen, Polonius, Ophelia, Rosencrantz and Guildenstern]
KING. Can you not find out, through any kind of indirect questioning, why he's putting on this confused behavior, ruining his peace with this turbulent and dangerous madness?
ROSENCRANTZ. He admits he feels distracted, but won't say why.
GUILDENSTERN. And we can't get him to open up. He keeps us at a distance with a kind of crafty madness whenever we try to get him to confess what's really going on.
QUEEN. Did he receive you well?
ROSENCRANTZ. Very politely, like a gentleman.
GUILDENSTERN. But he had to force himself to be friendly.
ROSENCRANTZ. He didn't ask us many questions, but he answered ours freely enough.
QUEEN. Did you try to interest him in any entertainment?

ROSENCRANTZ. It happened, madam, that we mentioned some actors we had passed on the road. He seemed to take a kind of pleasure in hearing about them. They're at court now, and I think they've already been asked to perform for him tonight.
POLONIUS. That's true, and he asked me to invite your Majesties to come and see the show.
KING. With all my heart — it pleases me greatly to hear he's interested in something. Good gentlemen, encourage him further and push him toward these pleasures.
ROSENCRANTZ. We will, my lord.
[Exeunt Rosencrantz and Guildenstern.]

KING. Dear Gertrude, leave us too. We've secretly arranged for Hamlet to come here as if by accident, where he'll run into Ophelia. Her father and I — perfectly justified in spying — will position ourselves where we can see without being seen, and openly judge from his behavior whether it's the affliction of love or something else that's making him suffer.
QUEEN. I'll do as you ask. And Ophelia, I hope that your beauty is the real cause of Hamlet's wildness, so that your virtue might restore him to his former self, to the honor of you both.
OPHELIA. I hope so too, madam.
[Exit Queen.]

POLONIUS. Ophelia, walk here. — Your Majesty, we'll hide ourselves. — [To Ophelia.] Read this prayer book, so the appearance of devotion can explain why you're alone here. It's something we're often guilty of — putting on a pious face to cover up devilish intentions.

KING. [Aside.] How painfully true that is! Those words sting my conscience. The painted cheek of a prostitute, covered in makeup, is no uglier compared to what's beneath it than my actions are compared to my fine-sounding words. What a heavy burden!
POLONIUS. I hear him coming. Let's withdraw, my lord.
[Exeunt King and Polonius.]
[Enter Hamlet]

HAMLET. To be, or not to be — that is the question. Is it nobler to endure the attacks and insults of outrageous fortune, or to take up arms against a sea of troubles and, by fighting, end them? To die — to sleep, nothing more. And by sleeping, to say we end the heartache and the thousand natural shocks that human flesh is subject to — that's a conclusion devoutly to be wished for. To die, to sleep. To sleep — and maybe to dream. Yes, there's the problem. Because in that sleep of death, what dreams might come after we've shed this mortal body must give us pause. That's what makes us endure misery for so long. For who would bear the whips and insults of time — the oppressor's cruelty, the proud man's contempt, the agony of unreturned love, the slowness of the law, the arrogance of those in power, and the abuse that patient, deserving people take from the unworthy — when he could simply end it all with a dagger? Who would carry these burdens, grunting and sweating under a weary life, if it weren't for the dread of something after death — that undiscovered country from which no traveler returns? That fear confuses our will and makes us endure the miseries we know rather than rush toward unknown ones. And so our conscience makes cowards of us all. The natural color of courage gets sickened over with the pale cast of too much thinking, and plans of great importance lose their momentum and never become action. But wait — here comes the beautiful Ophelia! — In your prayers, remember all my sins.
OPHELIA. My lord, how have you been these many days?
HAMLET. I humbly thank you — well, well, well.
OPHELIA. My lord, I have some keepsakes of yours that I've wanted to return for a long time. Please, take them back now.
HAMLET. No, not me — I never gave you anything.

OPHELIA. My lord, you know very well you did. And with them came words so sweetly spoken that they made the gifts more precious. Now that sweetness is gone — take them back. To a noble mind, rich gifts lose their value when the giver proves unkind. Here, my lord.
HAMLET. Ha! Are you virtuous?
OPHELIA. My lord?
HAMLET. Are you beautiful?
OPHELIA. What do you mean, my lord?
HAMLET. That if you're both virtuous and beautiful, your virtue should have nothing to do with your beauty.
OPHELIA. Could beauty have a better companion than virtue?

HAMLET. Absolutely — because the power of beauty will corrupt virtue into something base sooner than virtue can make beauty honest. That used to be a paradox, but now our times prove it. I did love you once.
OPHELIA. Indeed, my lord, you made me believe so.
HAMLET. You shouldn't have believed me. Virtue can't purify our corrupt nature completely — we'll always taste the original sin. I did not love you.
OPHELIA. Then I was truly deceived.

HAMLET. Get yourself to a convent. Why would you want to be a breeder of sinners? I'm reasonably honest myself, yet I could accuse myself of such things that it would have been better if my mother had never given birth to me. I am proud, vengeful, ambitious — with more offenses ready to hand than I have thoughts to hold them, imagination to shape them, or time to carry them out. What should someone like me be doing, crawling between heaven and earth? We are all complete villains — believe none of us. Go to a convent. Where is your father?
OPHELIA. At home, my lord.
HAMLET. Lock the doors on him, so he can play the fool only in his own house. Farewell.
OPHELIA. Oh, help him, kind heavens!

HAMLET. If you do marry, I'll give you this curse as your dowry: be as pure as ice, as clean as snow — you still won't escape slander. Get to a convent — go. Farewell. Or, if you insist on getting married, marry a fool — because wise men know only too well what monsters you women make of them. To a convent, go — and quickly. Farewell.
OPHELIA. Oh heavenly powers, restore his mind!

HAMLET. I've heard all about your painting too — how God gives you one face and you make yourselves another. You dance, you sway, you talk in that affected way, and you give cute nicknames to God's creatures, and you pretend your wanton behavior is just innocence. Enough — it's driven me mad. I tell you, there will be no more marriages. Those who are already married — all but one — shall live. The rest will stay single. To a convent, go.
[Exit.]

OPHELIA. Oh, what a noble mind has been destroyed! The perfect courtier, soldier, and scholar — the hope and ornament of our country, the mirror of fashion, the model of form, the one everyone watched and admired — completely, completely ruined! And I, the most miserable of women, who drank the honey of his beautiful promises — now I see that noble and supreme reason jangling like broken bells, harsh and out of tune. That matchless form and spirit of glowing youth, blasted by madness. Oh, what misery, to have seen what I once saw and now see what I see.
[Enter King and Polonius]

KING. Love? His feelings don't seem to run in that direction. What he said, though it was somewhat disordered, didn't sound like madness. There's something in his soul that his melancholy is brooding on, and I'm afraid that when it hatches, it will be dangerous. To prevent that, I've made a quick decision: he'll be sent to England immediately to demand payment of overdue tribute. Hopefully, different seas and countries, with their varied sights, will drive away whatever is lodged in his heart that's putting his mind so far out of balance. What do you think?

POLONIUS. That may work. But I still believe the root of his grief is unrequited love. Well, Ophelia? You don't need to tell us what Lord Hamlet said — we heard everything. My lord, do as you think best. But if you agree, after the play tonight, let his mother the Queen speak with him alone and try to get him to reveal what's troubling him. Let her be direct with him. And I'll hide where I can hear every word. If she can't get through to him, then send him to England, or confine him wherever your wisdom decides.
KING. So be it. Madness in powerful people must never go unwatched.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 2 — A Hall in the Castle
paragraphs: [Enter Hamlet and certain Players]

HAMLET. Deliver the speech, please, the way I taught it to you — naturally and smoothly. But if you start shouting it, I'd just as soon have the town crier read my lines. And don't wave your arms around too much — use restraint. Even in the middle of the most powerful storm of emotion, you must find a smoothness and control. It pains me to hear some blustering, wig-wearing fellow tear a speech to shreds, splitting the ears of the audience, who mostly can only appreciate pointless spectacle and noise. I'd have such a man whipped for overacting. It out-Herods Herod. Please avoid that.
FIRST PLAYER. I promise, my lord.

HAMLET. But don't be too tame either. Let your own good judgment guide you. Match the action to the words and the words to the action, with this one rule: don't overdo it. Because anything overdone defeats the whole purpose of acting, which has always been to hold a mirror up to nature — to show virtue its own reflection, foolishness its own image, and each era its true character. Now, if you overdo it or underplay it, even though it might make ignorant people laugh, it will make anyone with taste groan — and the opinion of one such person should outweigh that of a whole theater of others. There are actors I've seen — and heard praised highly — who, not to put too fine a point on it, didn't walk, talk, or behave like Christians, or even like human beings, but strutted and bellowed so badly that I thought some of nature's less talented craftsmen must have made them, they imitated humanity so poorly.
FIRST PLAYER. I hope we've more or less corrected that among ourselves, sir.

HAMLET. Correct it completely. And make sure the comedians stick to their scripts. Some of them will start improvising to get cheap laughs from the dullest part of the audience, right when something important is happening in the play. That's contemptible, and shows a pathetic kind of ambition in the fool who does it. Go get ready.
[Exeunt Players.]
[Enter Polonius, Rosencrantz and Guildenstern]
HAMLET. Well, my lord? Will the King see this performance?
POLONIUS. And the Queen too — right away.
HAMLET. Tell the players to hurry.
[Exit Polonius.]
HAMLET. Will you two help speed them along? ROSENCRANTZ and GUILDENSTERN. We will, my lord.
[Exeunt Rosencrantz and Guildenstern.]
HAMLET. Horatio!
[Enter Horatio]
HORATIO. Here, my sweet lord, at your service.
HAMLET. Horatio, you are the most honest and just man I've ever known.
HORATIO. Oh, my dear lord —

HAMLET. No, don't think I'm flattering you. What could I possibly gain from you? You have no income, nothing but your good character to sustain you. Why would anyone flatter a poor man? No — let fawning tongues lick the boots of absurd power and bend their knees wherever there's profit in groveling. Listen to me: ever since my soul was capable of choosing its friends, it has chosen you. Because you have been a person who, while enduring everything, suffers nothing — a man who has taken both the blows and the gifts of fortune with equal grace. Blessed are those whose emotions and judgment are so well balanced that they are not a pipe for fortune to play whatever tune she pleases on. Give me a man who is not a slave to his emotions, and I will hold him in my heart of hearts — as I hold you. But enough of that. There's a play tonight before the King.
