One scene in it closely mirrors the circumstances of my father's death, as I told you. Please, when you see that scene, watch my uncle with the sharpest attention of your soul. If his hidden guilt doesn't reveal itself during one particular speech, then the ghost we saw was a devil, and my suspicions are as foul as a blacksmith's forge. Watch him closely — I'll have my eyes locked on his face — and afterward we'll compare our judgments.
HORATIO. My lord, if he steals any reaction during this play and I miss it, I'll pay the price.
HAMLET. They're coming to the play. I need to act strange. Go find your seat.
[Danish march. A flourish. Enter King, Queen, Polonius, Ophelia,]
HAMLET. Rosencrantz, Guildenstern and others.
KING. How is our nephew Hamlet doing?
HAMLET. Excellently, thank you — I eat nothing but air, stuffed full of promises. You can't feed chickens like that.
KING. I don't know what to make of that answer, Hamlet. Those words mean nothing to me.
HAMLET. Nor to me, anymore. [To Polonius.] My lord, you once acted in a university play, you say?
POLONIUS. I did, my lord, and I was considered a good actor.
HAMLET. What role did you play?
POLONIUS. I played Julius Caesar. I was killed in the Capitol. Brutus killed me.
HAMLET. That was a brutal thing for him to do, killing such a prize calf in such a capital place. Are the players ready?
ROSENCRANTZ. Yes, my lord — they're waiting for you.
QUEEN. Come here, dear Hamlet. Sit next to me.
HAMLET. No, good mother — here's something more attractive.
POLONIUS. [To the King.] Oh ho! Did you notice that?
HAMLET. Lady, may I lie in your lap?
[Lying down at Ophelia's feet.]
OPHELIA. No, my lord.
HAMLET. I mean, may I rest my head on your lap?
OPHELIA. Yes, my lord.
HAMLET. Did you think I meant something indecent?
OPHELIA. I think nothing, my lord.
HAMLET. That's a good thing to have between a girl's legs.
OPHELIA. What is, my lord?
HAMLET. Nothing.
OPHELIA. You're in a good mood, my lord.
HAMLET. Who, me?
OPHELIA. Yes, my lord.
HAMLET. Oh God, I'm the ultimate entertainer! What else should a man do but be merry? Look how cheerful my mother looks, and my father died less than two hours ago.
OPHELIA. No, it's been four months, my lord.

HAMLET. That long? Well then, let the devil wear black — I'll have a suit of fine fur. Heavens — dead two months and not forgotten yet? Then there's hope that a great man's memory can outlive his life by half a year. But he'd better build churches, or else nobody will think of him at all — just like the hobby-horse, whose motto is 'The hobby-horse is forgotten!'
[Trumpets sound. The dumb show enters]

[Enter a King and a Queen very lovingly; the Queen embracing him and he her. She kneels, and makes show of protestation unto him. He takes her up, and declines his head upon her neck. Lays him down upon a bank of flowers. She, seeing him asleep, leaves him. Anon comes in a fellow, takes off his crown, kisses it, pours poison in the King's ears, and exits. The Queen returns, finds the King dead, and makes passionate action. The Poisoner with some three or four Mutes, comes in again, seeming to lament with her. The dead body is carried away. The Poisoner woos the Queen with gifts. She seems loth and unwilling awhile, but in the end accepts his love]
[Exeunt.]
OPHELIA. What does this mean, my lord?
HAMLET. It means mischief — sneaky mischief.
OPHELIA. Maybe this pantomime explains what the play is about.
[Enter Prologue]
HAMLET. We'll find out from this fellow. Actors can't keep a secret — they'll tell everything.
OPHELIA. Will he tell us what that pantomime meant?
HAMLET. Yes — or anything else you'd show him. Don't be shy about showing, and he won't be shy about telling.
OPHELIA. You're naughty. I'll just watch the play.
PROLOGUE. To you and to our play, here kneeling humbly, we beg your patient hearing.
HAMLET. Is this a prologue, or the inscription on a ring?
OPHELIA. It's brief, my lord.
HAMLET. As brief as a woman's love.
[Enter a King and a Queen]

PLAYER KING. Thirty times has the sun made its circuit around the salty seas and the round earth, and thirty dozen moons have lit the world twelve times thirty nights, since love joined our hearts and marriage joined our hands in sacred union.

PLAYER QUEEN. May we count as many more journeys of the sun and moon before our love is done. But I'm so worried about you — you've been so ill lately, so changed from your former self, that I'm filled with fear. Yet my worry must not distress you, my lord. A woman's fear and love are proportional — either both are nothing, or both are everything. My love has proven itself, and my fear matches it. Where love is great, even the smallest doubts feel enormous. Where fears are small, love has room to grow.
PLAYER KING. My love, I must leave you soon. My body's powers are failing me. You shall live on in this fair world, honored, beloved, and perhaps with a husband as kind as —
PLAYER QUEEN. Oh, don't say such things! Any love like that would be treason in my heart. May I be cursed if I take a second husband! Only the woman who killed her first husband marries a second one.
HAMLET. [Aside.] Bitter, bitter.
PLAYER QUEEN. A second marriage is motivated by money, not by love. Every time my second husband kisses me in bed, I kill my first husband all over again.

PLAYER KING. I believe you mean what you say now. But we so often break what we resolve to do. Intentions are just slaves to memory — born in violence but weak in staying power. Like unripe fruit that sticks to the tree but falls on its own when it's ripe. We inevitably forget to pay ourselves what we've promised. What we propose in passion, we abandon when the passion fades. Both extreme grief and extreme joy destroy their own resolutions. Where joy is greatest, grief waits nearby. Grief turns to joy and joy to grief at the slightest chance. This world doesn't last forever, and it shouldn't surprise us that our love changes with our fortune. Does love lead fortune, or fortune lead love? When a great man falls, you can watch his favorites scatter. When a poor man rises, he makes friends of his former enemies. That's how love follows fortune: a man who doesn't need help will never lack friends, but a man in need who tries to lean on a hollow friend quickly discovers an enemy instead. To conclude where I began: our wishes and our fates run so contrary to each other that our plans are always overturned. Our thoughts are ours, but their outcomes are not. So you may think you'll never take a second husband — but those thoughts will die when your first husband does.

PLAYER QUEEN. May the earth give me no food and heaven no light. May rest and comfort flee from me day and night. May hope turn to despair, and prison be my home. May every opposite of joy destroy what I wish for! May I suffer endlessly, here and in the afterlife, if I ever marry again after becoming a widow.
HAMLET. [To Ophelia.] What if she breaks this vow now?
PLAYER KING. That's a deep oath. Sweet, leave me here a while. My spirits are growing dull, and I'd like to pass this tedious day with sleep.
[Sleeps.]
PLAYER QUEEN. Sleep peacefully, and may nothing bad ever come between us.
[Exit.]
HAMLET. Madam, how do you like this play?
QUEEN. The lady protests too much, I think.
HAMLET. Oh, but she'll keep her word.
KING. Have you heard the plot? Is there anything offensive in it?
HAMLET. No, no — they're just acting. Poison in jest. No offense at all.
KING. What's the play called?

HAMLET. The Mousetrap. How's that for a title? Metaphorically, of course. This play depicts a murder committed in Vienna. Gonzago is the duke's name; his wife is Baptista. You'll see soon enough. It's a wicked piece of work — but so what? Your Majesty and those of us with clear consciences have nothing to worry about. Let the guilty horse wince — we have nothing to hide.
[Enter Lucianus]
HAMLET. This is Lucianus, nephew to the King.
OPHELIA. You make a good narrator, my lord.
HAMLET. I could narrate the love between you and your sweetheart, if I could see the puppets in action.
OPHELIA. You're sharp, my lord, you're sharp.
HAMLET. It would cost you a groan to dull my edge.
OPHELIA. Better and worse.
HAMLET. That's how women take their husbands — for better and worse. — Begin, murderer! Enough with the ugly faces — get on with it. Come on — the raven croaks for revenge.

LUCIANUS. Thoughts black, hands ready, poison prepared, and the moment right — with no witnesses, and the season as my accomplice. You vile mixture, brewed from midnight weeds, three times cursed and three times infected — let your deadly nature seize this wholesome life immediately.
[Pours the poison into the sleeper's ears.]

HAMLET. He poisons him in the garden to take his estate. His name is Gonzago. The story actually exists, written in elegant Italian. You're about to see how the murderer wins the love of Gonzago's wife.
OPHELIA. The King is rising!
HAMLET. What — frightened by a stage trick?
QUEEN. How are you, my lord?
POLONIUS. Stop the play!
KING. Bring me some light! Away! All. Lights, lights, lights!
[Exeunt all but Hamlet and Horatio.]

HAMLET. Well! Let the wounded deer weep while the unharmed deer plays. Some must watch while others sleep — that's the way the world goes. Wouldn't this performance, sir, plus a feathered hat, if my other fortunes turned on me — with a couple of fancy roses on my shoes — earn me a spot in a troupe of actors?
HORATIO. Half a share, maybe.
HAMLET. A whole one, I'd say! For you know, dear friend, this kingdom was stripped of its rightful ruler, and now a mere — peacock — reigns here.
HORATIO. You could have found a better rhyme.
HAMLET. Oh, good Horatio, I'd bet a thousand pounds on the ghost's word. Did you see it?
HORATIO. I did, my lord.
HAMLET. When the poisoning was mentioned?
HORATIO. I watched him very carefully.
HAMLET. Yes! Come, let's have some music! Bring the recorders! Because if the King doesn't like the comedy, well then — I guess he just doesn't like it. Come, some music!
[Enter Rosencrantz and Guildenstern]
GUILDENSTERN. My lord, may I have a word with you?
HAMLET. Sir, you can have a whole story.
GUILDENSTERN. The King, sir —
HAMLET. Yes, sir? What about him?
GUILDENSTERN. Has withdrawn to his chambers, very upset.
HAMLET. From drinking, sir?
GUILDENSTERN. No, my lord — from anger.
HAMLET. You'd be wiser to tell his doctor that. If I were to try to purge him, it might make him even angrier.
GUILDENSTERN. My lord, please make some sense of what you're saying, and don't veer so wildly away from the topic.
HAMLET. I'm perfectly calm, sir. Go ahead.
GUILDENSTERN. The Queen, your mother, in great distress of spirit, has sent me to you.
HAMLET. You're welcome.

GUILDENSTERN. No, my lord — this politeness isn't what's needed. If you'll give me a straight answer, I'll carry out your mother's request. If not, your forgiveness and my departure will end our business.
HAMLET. Sir, I can't.
GUILDENSTERN. Can't what, my lord?
HAMLET. Give you a straight answer — my mind is unwell. But I'll give you the best answer I can — or rather, as you say, what my mother wants. So, no more preamble. My mother, you say —
ROSENCRANTZ. She says this: your behavior has shocked and amazed her.
HAMLET. Oh, what a wonderful son, who can astonish his mother like that! But is there anything else behind her amazement?
ROSENCRANTZ. She wants to speak with you in her private room before you go to bed.
HAMLET. I'll obey her, even if she were ten times my mother. Is there anything else?
ROSENCRANTZ. My lord, you once cared for me.
HAMLET. And I still do, I swear by these honest hands.
ROSENCRANTZ. My lord, what's the cause of your distress? You're essentially locking yourself up by refusing to confide your troubles to your friends.
HAMLET. Sir, I lack advancement.
ROSENCRANTZ. How can that be, when the King himself has named you as his successor in Denmark?
HAMLET. Yes, sir, but 'while the grass grows' — as the saying goes, and it's getting a bit stale.
[Re-enter the Players with recorders]
HAMLET. Oh — the recorders. Let me see one. — Now, why are you circling around me like hunters trying to drive me into a trap?
GUILDENSTERN. Oh my lord, if my devotion seems too bold, it's only because my love knows no manners.
HAMLET. I don't quite follow that. Will you play this recorder?
GUILDENSTERN. My lord, I can't.
HAMLET. Please.
GUILDENSTERN. Believe me, I can't.
HAMLET. I beg you.
GUILDENSTERN. I have no idea how to play it, my lord.
HAMLET. It's as easy as lying. Cover these holes with your fingers and thumb, blow into it with your mouth, and it will produce the most eloquent music. See — these are the stops.
GUILDENSTERN. But I can't make it produce any harmony. I don't have the skill.

HAMLET. Well, look at how little you think of me! You'd play on me — you'd pretend to know my inner workings, you'd pluck out the heart of my mystery, you'd sound me from my lowest note to my highest — and yet there is excellent music and voice in this little instrument, and you can't make it speak. Do you think I'm easier to play than a pipe? Call me whatever instrument you like — though you can irritate me, you cannot play me.
[Enter Polonius]
HAMLET. God bless you, sir.
POLONIUS. My lord, the Queen wishes to speak with you, right away.
HAMLET. Do you see that cloud that looks almost like a camel?
POLONIUS. By heaven, it does look like a camel.
HAMLET. I think it looks like a weasel.
POLONIUS. It does have a weasel-like shape.
HAMLET. Or like a whale.
POLONIUS. Very much like a whale.
HAMLET. Then I'll go to my mother shortly. — They push me to the limit of my patience. — I'll come shortly.
POLONIUS. I'll tell her so.
[Exit.]
HAMLET. 'Shortly' is easy to say. Leave me, friends.
[Exeunt all but Hamlet.]

HAMLET. It's now the very witching hour of night, when graveyards open and hell breathes its infection into the world. Right now I could drink hot blood and do the kind of terrible things that daylight would shudder to witness. But wait — I'm going to my mother. My heart, don't lose your humanity. Don't let the soul of the tyrant Nero enter this body. Let me be cruel, but not unnatural. I'll speak daggers to her, but use none. My words and my soul will be at odds — however much my words may wound her, let me never act on them.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 3 — A Room in the Castle
paragraphs: [Enter King, Rosencrantz and Guildenstern]

KING. I don't like him, and it's not safe for us to let his madness run loose. Get ready — I'm drawing up your commission immediately. He'll go to England with you. The security of our state cannot tolerate this kind of danger growing so close to us, hour by hour.
GUILDENSTERN. We'll prepare at once. It's a sacred and religious duty to protect the many lives that depend on your Majesty.

ROSENCRANTZ. Every individual person is duty-bound to protect themselves with all their mental strength and will. But how much more so the person upon whose well-being so many other lives depend. When a king falls, it's like a massive wheel fixed to the highest peak — when it falls, every small thing attached to it comes crashing down too. A king never sighs alone — it causes a universal groan.
KING. Get ready, please, for this quick voyage. We need to put chains on this danger that now roams too freely. ROSENCRANTZ and GUILDENSTERN. We'll make haste.
[Exeunt Rosencrantz and Guildenstern.]
[Enter Polonius]

POLONIUS. My lord, he's on his way to his mother's room. I'll hide behind the tapestry to overhear their conversation. I'm sure she'll confront him firmly. And as you wisely said, it's appropriate that someone besides a mother — since nature makes mothers partial — should listen in. Farewell, my lord. I'll report to you before you go to bed and tell you what I've learned.
KING. Thank you, my dear lord.
[Exit Polonius.]

KING. Oh, my offense is vile — it stinks to heaven. It bears the oldest curse of all — a brother's murder! I cannot pray, though my desire to pray is as sharp as my will. My stronger guilt defeats my strong intention, and, like a man pulled in two directions at once, I stand paralyzed, unable to begin, and both tasks left undone. What if this cursed hand were thicker than itself with brother's blood — isn't there enough rain in all the sweet heavens to wash it white as snow? What's the purpose of mercy if not to confront the face of sin? And what is prayer's power if not this double force: to prevent us from falling, or to pardon us once we've fallen? Then I'll look up. My sin is in the past. But oh — what form of prayer can help me? 'Forgive me my foul murder'? That cannot be, since I still possess everything I murdered to get — my crown, my ambition, and my queen. Can a person be pardoned while still holding the profits of the crime? In the corrupt currents of this world, a criminal's gold-tipped hand can push justice aside, and often the stolen prize itself buys off the law. But it's not that way in heaven. There, you can't cheat — the case is tried in its true nature, and we are forced to confront our faults face to face and give testimony against ourselves. What then? What's left? Try what repentance can do. What can't it do? Yet what use is it when one cannot repent? Oh, wretched state! Oh, heart as black as death! Oh, soul trapped like a bird in lime — the more you struggle to be free, the more tangled you become! Help, angels! Let me try. Bow, stubborn knees, and heart with strings of steel, become as soft as a newborn baby's. All may yet be well.
[Retires and kneels.]
[Enter Hamlet]

HAMLET. Now I could do it — right now, while he's praying. And now I'll do it. And so he goes straight to heaven. And that's my revenge? That needs more thought. A villain murders my father, and for that I, his only son, send that same villain to heaven. No — that's a reward, not revenge. He killed my father while my father was unprepared — full of earthly pleasures, with all his sins in full bloom. And what his account looks like before God, only heaven knows — but by our way of thinking, it weighs heavily against him. And would it be revenge to kill him while he's purifying his soul, when he's prepared and ready for death? No. Sword, wait for a more terrible opportunity: when he's passed out drunk, or in a rage, or in the pleasure of his incestuous bed, or gambling, or swearing, or doing something that has no trace of salvation in it. Then strike him down, so his heels may kick at heaven and his soul be as damned and black as hell, where it will go. My mother is waiting. This praying only extends your numbered days.
[Exit.]
HAMLET. The King rises and advances.
KING. My words fly up, but my thoughts stay below. Words without thoughts never reach heaven.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 4 — Another Room in the Castle
paragraphs: [Enter Queen and Polonius]

POLONIUS. He'll be here any moment. Make sure you lay into him. Tell him his antics have gone too far, and that you have shielded him from the King's anger. I'll stay quiet right here behind the curtain. Be direct with him.
HAMLET. [Within.] Mother, mother, mother!
QUEEN. Don't worry — I can handle him. Hide — I hear him coming.
[Polonius goes behind the arras.]
[Enter Hamlet]
HAMLET. Now, mother — what's the matter?
QUEEN. Hamlet, you have deeply offended your father.
HAMLET. Mother, you have deeply offended my father.
QUEEN. Come, come — you're speaking nonsense.
HAMLET. Go, go — you're asking a wicked question.
QUEEN. What's gotten into you, Hamlet?
HAMLET. What's the matter now?
QUEEN. Have you forgotten who I am?
HAMLET. No, by the cross, I haven't. You are the Queen — your husband's brother's wife. And — I wish you weren't — you are my mother.
QUEEN. Fine, then I'll send someone who can talk to you.
HAMLET. Come, come — sit down. You're not moving from this spot. I'm going to hold up a mirror so you can see yourself for what you really are.
QUEEN. What are you going to do? You're not going to murder me? Help! Help!
POLONIUS. [Behind.] Help! Help! Help!
HAMLET. What? A rat? [Draws his sword.] Dead, for a dollar — dead!
[Makes a pass through the arras.]
POLONIUS. [Behind.] Oh — I'm killed!
[Falls and dies.]
QUEEN. Oh God, what have you done?
HAMLET. I don't know. Is it the King?
[Draws forth Polonius.]
QUEEN. Oh, what a reckless and bloody deed!
HAMLET. A bloody deed — almost as bad, good mother, as killing a king and marrying his brother.
QUEEN. As killing a king?

HAMLET. Yes, lady, that's what I said. — [To Polonius.] You wretched, rash, meddling fool — farewell! I mistook you for your superior. Accept your fate — you've learned that being too nosy is dangerous. — Stop wringing your hands. Sit down and let me wring your heart, because I will — if it hasn't grown so hardened by wicked habit that it's impervious to feeling.
QUEEN. What have I done that you dare speak to me so harshly?

HAMLET. An act that stains the grace and blush of modesty, makes virtue a hypocrite, strips the rose from the forehead of innocent love and sets a blister there instead. An act that makes marriage vows as false as a gambler's oaths. Oh, such a deed as rips the very soul from the body of a sacred contract and turns religion into a jumble of empty words. Heaven's face itself burns with shame, and even the solid earth looks as sick and sorrowful as if doomsday were coming, disgusted by the act.
QUEEN. What act, that thunders so loudly even in the introduction?

HAMLET. Look at this picture, and now at this — portraits of two brothers. See what grace sat on this brow — the curls of a sun god, the forehead of Jove himself, eyes like Mars commanding with authority, a bearing like Mercury, the winged messenger of the gods, newly landed on a heaven-kissing hill. A combination where every god seemed to set his seal, guaranteeing the world: this is a man. This was your husband. Now look at the next one. Here is your husband — like a diseased ear of corn, blighting his wholesome brother. Do you have eyes? Could you leave this beautiful mountain to graze in this swamp? Do you have eyes? You can't call it love — at your age, passion has calmed down and waits upon judgment. And what kind of judgment would step from this to that? Your senses must be paralyzed — because even madness wouldn't make such an error, and no sense was ever so enslaved to insanity that it couldn't retain some ability to choose between such different options. What devil tricked you in this blindfold game? Eyes without feeling, feeling without sight, hearing without hands or eyes, smell without anything else, or even a sick fragment of one true sense, could not be so deluded. Oh shame — where is your blush? If rebellion can burn in a mature woman's bones, then let virtue melt like wax in the heat of flaming youth. Don't bother calling anything shameful when overpowering lust takes the lead, since even frost burns with equal passion, and reason becomes the servant of desire.
QUEEN. Oh Hamlet, say no more! You're turning my eyes inward toward my very soul, and there I see stains so deep and dark they will never come out.
HAMLET. No — to live in the rank sweat of a greasy bed, stewing in corruption, making love in a disgusting pigsty —
QUEEN. Don't say any more. These words enter my ears like daggers. No more, sweet Hamlet!

HAMLET. A murderer and a villain — a slave who isn't a twentieth of the man your former husband was. A clown king, a pickpocket of the empire, who stole the precious crown from its shelf and put it in his pocket!
QUEEN. No more!
HAMLET. A king of rags and patches! —
[Enter Ghost]
HAMLET. Save me! Spread your wings over me, you heavenly guards! What do you want, gracious spirit?
QUEEN. He's gone mad!
HAMLET. Have you come to scold your tardy son, who has let time and emotion slip by without carrying out your dread command? Tell me!

GHOST. Don't forget. This visit is only to sharpen your nearly blunted purpose. But look — amazement has paralyzed your mother. Step between her and her struggling soul — the imagination works most powerfully in the weakest bodies. Speak to her, Hamlet.
HAMLET. How are you, lady?

QUEEN. How are you, rather? You're staring at empty air and talking to nothing! Your eyes are wild and staring, and your hair, like sleeping soldiers woken by an alarm, is standing straight on end. Oh, gentle son — sprinkle cool patience on the heat and flame of your madness. What are you looking at?

HAMLET. At him — at him! Look how pale he is! His form and his purpose together, preaching to stones, would make them capable of feeling. — Don't look at me like that, or your pitiful expression will weaken my resolve. Then what I have to do will lose its true character — I might shed tears instead of blood.
QUEEN. Who are you talking to?
HAMLET. Do you see nothing there?
QUEEN. Nothing at all — and yet I see everything that's there.
HAMLET. And you heard nothing?
QUEEN. No, nothing but ourselves.
HAMLET. Why — look there! See how it moves away! My father, dressed as he was in life! Look — there he goes, right now, out through the doorway!
[Exit Ghost.]
QUEEN. This is purely a creation of your disturbed brain. Madness is very skilled at producing these kinds of hallucinations.

HAMLET. Madness? My pulse beats as steadily as yours, keeping healthy time. What I've said is not madness. Test me — I'll repeat it word for word. Madness would scramble everything. Mother, for the love of God, don't comfort your soul with the flattering belief that it's my madness speaking and not your own guilt. That would only put a thin skin over the ulcerous wound, while the rot keeps spreading underneath. Confess to heaven. Repent what's past. Avoid what's to come. And don't fertilize the weeds to make them grow even thicker. Forgive me for this moralizing — in these bloated times, virtue itself must beg vice for permission to do good.
QUEEN. Oh Hamlet, you have split my heart in two!

HAMLET. Then throw away the worse half and live more purely with the better one. Good night. But don't go to my uncle's bed. Adopt virtue, even if you don't feel it naturally. The monster of habit, which devours all natural feeling when it comes to evil, is an angel in this respect: that it also makes a costume of good actions that becomes easier and easier to wear. Resist tonight, and that will make tomorrow's resistance easier. The next time easier still. Because habit can almost change our very nature, mastering the devil or throwing him out with remarkable power. Once more, good night. And when you're ready to be blessed, I'll ask for your blessing. As for this lord —
[Pointing to Polonius.]

HAMLET. I'm sorry. But heaven has chosen to punish me through him and him through me, making me its instrument of justice. I'll take care of the body and accept responsibility for his death. So again, good night. I must be cruel only to be kind. This is a bad beginning, and worse is yet to come. One more thing, good lady.
QUEEN. What should I do?

HAMLET. Absolutely not this, which I'm telling you to do: don't let the bloated King tempt you back to bed, pinch your cheek playfully, call you his pet name, and with his damned fingers on your neck and his filthy kisses, get you to reveal everything — that I'm not truly mad, but only pretending to be mad. It would be good to let him know — because what queen, fair, sensible, and wise, would hide such important matters from a toad, a bat, a tomcat? Who would do that? No — despite all sense and secrecy, don't open the cage on the rooftop, let the birds fly out, and then, like the famous ape, climb into the cage yourself and break your own neck.
QUEEN. You can be sure — if words are made of breath and breath of life — I have no life left to breathe a word of what you've said to me.
HAMLET. I have to go to England — you know that?
QUEEN. I'd forgotten! Yes, that's been decided.

HAMLET. There are sealed letters — and my two school friends, whom I trust about as far as I'd trust venomous snakes — they carry the orders and will escort me straight into a trap. Let it happen. There's a special pleasure in seeing the bomb-maker blown up by his own bomb. And it'll be a hard day when I can't dig a yard deeper than their tunnels and blow them sky-high. Oh, it's so satisfying when two schemes collide head-on. This man will get me moving. I'll drag the body into the next room. Mother, good night. Indeed, this advisor is now very still, very secret, and very grave — though in life he was a foolish, chattering fool. Come, sir, let me wrap things up with you. Good night, mother.
[Exit Hamlet dragging out Polonius.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 1 — A Room in the Castle
paragraphs: [Enter King, Queen, Rosencrantz and Guildenstern]
KING. These sighs mean something. These deep heaves — you must explain them. It's important that we understand. Where is your son?
QUEEN. Give us the room for a moment.
[To Rosencrantz and Guildenstern, who go out.]
QUEEN. Oh my lord, what I've seen tonight!
KING. What is it, Gertrude? What about Hamlet?

QUEEN. Mad as the sea and wind when they're fighting over which is stronger. In his wild fit, hearing something stir behind the curtain, he whipped out his sword, shouted 'A rat, a rat!' and in this deranged state killed the unseen old man hiding there.

KING. Oh, terrible deed! That could have been us if we had been there. His freedom is a threat to everyone — to you, to us, to the whole world. How will this bloody act be answered for? It will be blamed on us, since our love should have kept this dangerous young man restrained and out of harm's way. But we loved him so much that we refused to see what needed to be done, like the owner of a terrible disease who lets it feed on his own vitality rather than revealing it. Where has he gone?
QUEEN. To drag away the body of the man he killed. Even in his madness, like pure gold found among base metals, his goodness shows through. He weeps for what he's done.
KING. Oh Gertrude, come! As soon as the sun touches the mountains, we'll ship him away. And we must use all our authority and skill to both acknowledge and excuse this terrible act. — Guildenstern!
[Re-enter Rosencrantz and Guildenstern]

KING. Friends, go get help. Hamlet has killed Polonius in a fit of madness and dragged the body from his mother's room. Go find him, speak to him gently, and bring the body to the chapel. Please, hurry.
[Exeunt Rosencrantz and Guildenstern.]

KING. Come, Gertrude — we'll summon our wisest advisors and tell them what we plan to do and what has happened. Perhaps that way slander — whose whisper reaches across the world as straight as a cannonball to its target, carrying its poisonous shot — may miss our name and hit only the empty air. Oh, come away! My soul is full of conflict and dread.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 2 — Another Room in the Castle
paragraphs: [Enter Hamlet]
HAMLET. Safely hidden away. ROSENCRANTZ and GUILDENSTERN. [Within.] Hamlet! Lord Hamlet!
HAMLET. What's that noise? Who's calling for Hamlet? Oh, here they come.
[Enter Rosencrantz and Guildenstern]
ROSENCRANTZ. What have you done with the dead body, my lord?
HAMLET. Mixed it back with the dust it came from.
ROSENCRANTZ. Tell us where it is so we can take it to the chapel.
HAMLET. Don't count on it.
ROSENCRANTZ. Count on what?
HAMLET. That I can keep your secrets and not my own. Besides, to be questioned by a sponge — what kind of answer should a prince give?
ROSENCRANTZ. You think I'm a sponge, my lord?

HAMLET. Yes, sir — one that soaks up the King's favor, his rewards, and his authority. But people like you serve the King best in the end: he keeps you, like an ape keeps food in the corner of its mouth — first chewed, then swallowed last. When he needs what you've absorbed, he just squeezes you dry.
ROSENCRANTZ. I don't understand you, my lord.
HAMLET. I'm glad of it. A clever remark is wasted on a foolish ear.
ROSENCRANTZ. My lord, you must tell us where the body is and come with us to the King.
HAMLET. The body is with the King, but the King is not with the body. The King is a thing —
GUILDENSTERN. A thing, my lord?
HAMLET. Of nothing. Take me to him. Come on — hide and seek!
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 3 — Another Room in the Castle
paragraphs: [Enter King, attended]

KING. I've sent people to find him and locate the body. How dangerous it is that this man walks free! Yet we can't apply the full force of the law — he's loved by the confused masses, who judge with their eyes and not their minds. In such cases, the offender's punishment is noticed, but never the offense itself. To keep everything smooth and even, this sudden sending away must appear to be a carefully considered decision. Desperate diseases require desperate remedies — or no remedy at all.
[Enter Rosencrantz]
KING. Well? What happened?
ROSENCRANTZ. We can't get him to tell us where the body is, my lord.
KING. But where is he?
ROSENCRANTZ. Outside, my lord, under guard, waiting for your instructions.
KING. Bring him before us.
ROSENCRANTZ. Guildenstern! Bring in my lord.
[Enter Hamlet and Guildenstern]
KING. Now, Hamlet — where's Polonius?
HAMLET. At supper.
KING. At supper? Where?

HAMLET. Not where he's eating, but where he's being eaten. A congregation of politically-minded worms is feasting on him as we speak. Your worm is the only true emperor when it comes to diet. We fatten up all other creatures to fatten ourselves, and we fatten ourselves for the maggots. Your fat king and your skinny beggar are just different courses — two dishes at one table. That's how it ends.
KING. What a sad thought.
HAMLET. A man may fish with the worm that ate a king, and then eat the fish that fed on that worm.
KING. What do you mean by that?
HAMLET. Nothing — just showing you how a king can take a journey through the guts of a beggar.
KING. Where is Polonius?

HAMLET. In heaven. Send someone there to check. If your messenger can't find him there, try the other place yourself. But honestly — if you don't find him within a month, you'll smell him as you go up the stairs to the lobby.
KING. [To some Attendants.] Go look for him there.
HAMLET. He'll wait for you.
[Exeunt Attendants.]

KING. Hamlet, this act — for your own special safety, which we care about deeply, as much as we grieve for what you've done — requires us to send you away immediately. So prepare yourself. The ship is ready, the wind is favorable, your escorts are waiting, and everything is set for England.
HAMLET. For England?
KING. Yes, Hamlet.
HAMLET. Good.
KING. It is good, if you knew our intentions.
HAMLET. I see an angel who sees them. But come — off to England! Farewell, dear mother.
KING. Your loving father, Hamlet.
HAMLET. My mother. Father and mother are man and wife. Man and wife are one flesh. So — my mother. Come, on to England!
[Exit.]
KING. Follow close behind him. Get him on that ship tonight — don't delay. Everything else related to this matter is signed and sealed. I want him gone immediately. Hurry.
[Exeunt Rosencrantz and Guildenstern.]

KING. And England — if you value my friendship at all, as my power gives you reason to, since the scar from the Danish sword is still raw and red on you, and your fear of us still commands your obedience — you must not take my royal command lightly. These letters demand, in the strongest terms, the immediate execution of Hamlet. Do it, England — because he rages in my blood like a fever, and you must cure me. Until I know it's done, no matter what else happens, I can never be happy.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 4 — A Plain in Denmark
paragraphs: [Enter Fortinbras and Forces marching]

FORTINBRAS. Go, Captain. Give my greetings to the Danish king. Tell him that Fortinbras requests permission, as promised, to march his army across his kingdom. You know the meeting point. If his Majesty needs anything from us, we'll present ourselves to him in person. Let him know.
CAPTAIN. I will, my lord.
FORTINBRAS. March quietly on.
[Exeunt all but the Captain.]
[Enter Hamlet, Rosencrantz, Guildenstern &c]
HAMLET. Good sir, whose troops are these?
CAPTAIN. They belong to Norway, sir.
HAMLET. What's their mission?
CAPTAIN. They're marching against part of Poland.
HAMLET. Who commands them?
CAPTAIN. The nephew of the old King of Norway — Fortinbras.
HAMLET. Is it aimed at the heart of Poland, or just some border territory?

CAPTAIN. To tell the truth, with no exaggeration, we're going to capture a tiny patch of ground that has no value except its name. I wouldn't pay five ducats to farm it, and it wouldn't bring a better price if sold outright to Norway or Poland.
HAMLET. Then Poland will never bother defending it.
CAPTAIN. Actually, it's already garrisoned.

HAMLET. Two thousand lives and twenty thousand ducats won't settle this trivial dispute! This is the abscess that grows from too much wealth and peace — it bursts internally with no outward sign of why the patient dies. Thank you, sir.
CAPTAIN. God be with you, sir.
[Exit.]
ROSENCRANTZ. Shall we go, my lord?
HAMLET. I'll catch up with you. Go on ahead.
[Exeunt all but Hamlet.]

HAMLET. Everything I see accuses me and spurs on my sluggish revenge! What is a man if his greatest purpose is just sleeping and eating? A beast, nothing more. Surely the one who made us with such expansive reason — the ability to look forward and backward — didn't give us that godlike capacity just to let it rust unused. Now, whether it's animal-like forgetfulness, or some cowardly hesitation from thinking too precisely about consequences — a thought which, when examined, turns out to be one part wisdom and three parts cowardice — I don't know why I'm still alive saying 'This thing needs to be done' when I have the cause, the will, the strength, and the means to do it. Examples as plain as the earth itself urge me on. Look at this army of enormous size and expense, led by a delicate and tender prince whose spirit, swollen with divine ambition, laughs at the unforeseeable outcome, risking everything mortal and uncertain against all that fortune, death, and danger can throw at him — even for an eggshell. True greatness is not about refusing to act without a great cause, but about finding something worth fighting for even in the smallest insult, when honor is at stake. How do I stand, then — with a father murdered, a mother dishonored, provocations to both my reason and my passion — and yet I do nothing? While to my shame, I watch the imminent death of twenty thousand men who, for a fantasy and a bit of fame, march to their graves as easily as to their beds, fighting over a plot of ground too small to hold them all or even to bury the dead. From this moment on, let my thoughts be bloody or worthless.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 5 — Elsinore. A Room in the Castle
paragraphs: [Enter Queen, Horatio and a Gentleman]
QUEEN. I won't speak with her.
GENTLEMAN. She's very insistent — in fact, she's out of her mind. Her state demands pity.
QUEEN. What does she want?

GENTLEMAN. She talks a lot about her father. She says she hears there are plots afoot in the world. She wrings her hands, thumps her chest, is irrationally angry at trivial things, and speaks in a confused way that only half makes sense. Her speech is meaningless, yet its very confusion moves the listeners to piece it together. They try to make sense of it, and with her winks and nods and gestures, they construct meaning. It's nothing certain, but it's deeply unsettling. It would be wise to speak with her — she might plant dangerous suspicions in troubled minds.
QUEEN. Let her come in.
[Exit Gentleman.]

QUEEN. To my sick soul, as is the nature of guilt, every small thing feels like a prelude to some great catastrophe. Guilt is so full of clumsy anxiety that it spills itself in the very act of trying not to spill.
[Enter Ophelia]
OPHELIA. Where is the beautiful Queen of Denmark?
QUEEN. What is it, Ophelia?
[Sings.]
OPHELIA. How should I tell your true love from another one? By his pilgrim's hat and his walking staff and his sandals.
QUEEN. Oh dear, sweet lady — what does this song mean?
OPHELIA. What did you say? Listen carefully.
[Sings.]
OPHELIA. He is dead and gone, lady, he is dead and gone. At his head a patch of green grass, at his feet a stone.
QUEEN. But Ophelia —
OPHELIA. Please, listen.
[Sings.]
OPHELIA. White as mountain snow was his burial shroud.
[Enter King]
QUEEN. Oh no — look here, my lord!
[Sings.]
OPHELIA. Covered all with sweet flowers, which went to the grave unwept, without true-love's tears.
KING. How are you, pretty lady?
OPHELIA. Fine, God reward you! They say the owl was a baker's daughter. Lord, we know what we are, but we don't know what we might become. God be at your table!
KING. She's dwelling on her father.
OPHELIA. Please, let's not talk about this anymore. But when they ask you what it means, say this:
[Sings.]

OPHELIA. Tomorrow is Saint Valentine's day, early in the morning time, and I a maiden at your window, come to be your Valentine. Then up he got and put his clothes on, and opened up the bedroom door. He let the girl in as a maiden, but she never left one anymore.
KING. Poor Ophelia!
OPHELIA. Indeed — without an oath, I'll finish it.
[Sings.]

OPHELIA. By Jesus and by Saint Charity, oh, the shame of it! Young men will do it if they get the chance — truly, they are to blame. She said: Before you had me, you promised me you'd wed. And he said: So I would have, by the sun above, if you hadn't come to my bed.
KING. How long has she been like this?

OPHELIA. I hope everything will be fine. We must be patient. But I can't help weeping to think they laid him in the cold ground. My brother will hear about this. And so I thank you for your good advice. Come, my carriage! Good night, ladies. Good night, sweet ladies. Good night, good night.
[Exit.]
KING. Follow her closely and watch over her, please.
[Exit Horatio.]

KING. Oh, this is the poison of deep grief — it all springs from her father's death. Oh Gertrude, Gertrude — when sorrows come, they come not one at a time, but in whole armies. First, her father killed. Then your son, gone — and he himself the violent cause of his own banishment. The people are confused, thick with unwholesome thoughts and whispers about Polonius's death. And we were foolish to bury him in such secrecy and haste. Poor Ophelia, torn away from her own mind and good judgment — without which we are nothing more than pictures or mere animals. And finally, and just as serious as all the rest: her brother has secretly returned from France. He feeds on his bewilderment, keeps to the shadows, and has no shortage of gossips buzzing in his ear with poisonous stories about his father's death. These rumors, starved for real facts, won't hesitate to blame us directly. Oh, my dear Gertrude — all of this, like a weapon packed with scattered shot, is killing me over and over.
[A noise within.]
QUEEN. What's that noise?
KING. Where are my guards? Let them protect the door!
[Enter a Gentleman]
KING. What's happening?

GENTLEMAN. Save yourself, my lord! The ocean doesn't eat away the shore with more relentless force than young Laertes, at the head of a rioting mob, is overwhelming your officers. The rabble call him lord, and as if the world were starting over fresh — tradition forgotten, custom unknown, every established law thrown aside — they're shouting: 'We choose Laertes! Laertes shall be king!' Hats, hands, and voices applaud it to the skies: 'Laertes shall be king! Laertes king!'
QUEEN. How eagerly they chase the wrong trail! This is backwards, you treacherous Danish dogs!
[A noise within.]
KING. The doors have been broken down!
[Enter Laertes, armed; Danes following]
LAERTES. Where is this king? — You men — stand outside. Danes. No, let us come in!
LAERTES. Please, let me handle this. DANES. All right, all right.
[They retire without the door.]
LAERTES. Thank you. Guard the door. — You vile king! Give me my father!
QUEEN. Calm down, Laertes.
LAERTES. If there's a drop of calm blood in me, it proclaims me a bastard, calls my father a cuckold, and brands my honest mother a whore.

KING. What's the reason for this, Laertes, that your rebellion looks so enormous? — Let him go, Gertrude. Don't worry about my safety. There is a divine protection that hedges a king, so that treason can only peek at what it wants to do, acting out very little of its will. — Tell me, Laertes, why you're so angry. — Let him go, Gertrude. — Speak, man.
LAERTES. Where is my father?
KING. Dead.
QUEEN. But not by the King's hand.
KING. Let him ask whatever he wants.

LAERTES. How did he die? I won't be manipulated. To hell with loyalty! Vows, to the blackest devil! Conscience and grace, to the deepest pit! I don't care about damnation. I've reached the point where I don't care about this world or the next. Come what may — I will be thoroughly revenged for my father.
KING. Who's going to stop you?
LAERTES. My own will — not the whole world's. And as for my resources, I'll use them so efficiently that a little will go a long way.
KING. Good Laertes, if you want to know the truth about your dear father's death, does your revenge require you to sweep up both friends and enemies, winners and losers alike?
LAERTES. Only his enemies.
KING. Then you'll want to know who they are?
LAERTES. To his friends I'll open my arms wide and feed them with my own blood, like a self-sacrificing pelican.

KING. Now you sound like a good son and a true gentleman. That I am innocent of your father's death, and deeply grieved by it, will become as clear to your judgment as daylight is to your eyes. DANES. [Within.] Let her come in!
LAERTES. What's that noise?
[Re-enter Ophelia, fantastically dressed with straws and flowers]

LAERTES. Oh God — let my brains dry up! Let tears seven times as salty burn out my sight! By heaven, her madness will be paid back in full until the scales tip in our favor! Oh rose of May! Dear girl, kind sister, sweet Ophelia! Oh heavens — is it possible that a young woman's sanity could be as fragile as an old man's life? Human nature is so refined in love that when love is intense enough, it sends some precious part of itself after the thing it loves.
[Sings.]
OPHELIA. They carried him bare-faced on the funeral stretcher, hey nonny, nonny, hey nonny, and on his grave many tears were shed. — Farewell, my dove!
LAERTES. If you had your wits and were urging me to revenge, it couldn't move me like this.
OPHELIA. You have to sing 'Down a-down, and you call him a-down-a.' Oh, how the spinning wheel suits the song! It's the story of the false steward who stole his master's daughter.
LAERTES. This babble means more than sense would.
OPHELIA. Here's rosemary — that's for remembrance. Please, love, remember. And here are pansies — that's for thoughts.
LAERTES. A lesson in madness — thoughts and remembrance perfectly matched.

OPHELIA. Here's fennel for you, and columbines. Here's rue for you, and some for me too. We can call it the herb of grace on Sundays. But you must wear your rue differently from mine. Here's a daisy. I would give you some violets, but they all withered when my father died. They say he made a good end.
[Sings.]
OPHELIA. For pretty sweet Robin is all my joy.
LAERTES. Thought and suffering, passion, even hell itself — she turns them all into beauty and grace.
[Sings.]

OPHELIA. And will he not come again? And will he not come again? No, no, he is dead. Go to your deathbed. He never will come again. His beard was white as snow, his hair all flaxen white. He is gone, he is gone, and we mourn in vain. God have mercy on his soul. And on all Christian souls, I pray God. God be with you.
[Exit.]
LAERTES. Do you see this, God?

KING. Laertes, I must share in your grief, or you deny me my right. Step aside with me. Choose whichever of your wisest friends you want, and let them hear and judge between us. If by any direct or indirect involvement they find me guilty, I will give you our kingdom, our crown, our life, and everything we call ours as compensation. But if not, be willing to grant us your patience, and we will work together to give your soul the satisfaction it needs.

LAERTES. So be it. The manner of his death, his obscure burial — no monument, no sword of honor over his bones, no noble ceremony, no proper funeral — all of this cries out to be investigated, demanding an explanation as loud as a voice from heaven to earth.
KING. And you shall have your investigation. And wherever the guilt lies, let the great axe fall. Please, come with me.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 6 — Another Room in the Castle
paragraphs: [Enter Horatio and a Servant]
HORATIO. Who wants to speak with me? SERVANT. Some sailors, sir. They say they have letters for you.
HORATIO. Let them come in.
[Exit Servant.]
HORATIO. I can't imagine who'd be writing to me from abroad, unless it's from Lord Hamlet.
[Enter Sailors]
FIRST SAILOR. God bless you, sir.
HORATIO. And you as well.
FIRST SAILOR. He will, sir, God willing. Here's a letter for you, sir. It comes from the ambassador who was heading to England — if your name is Horatio, as I've been told it is.

HORATIO. [Reads.] 'Horatio — when you've read this, arrange for these men to get an audience with the King. They have letters for him. We were barely two days at sea when a pirate ship, well-armed for battle, gave us chase. Finding our ship too slow, we fought back out of necessity, and during the boarding I jumped onto their vessel. The instant I did, they broke free of our ship, so I alone became their prisoner. They've treated me like merciful thieves — but they knew what they were doing. I owe them a favor in return. Make sure the King gets the letters I've sent, and come to me as fast as if you were running from death itself. I have things to tell you that will strike you dumb, yet they're not weighty enough for what this situation requires. These men will bring you to where I am. Rosencrantz and Guildenstern are still on course for England — I have much to tell you about them. Farewell. He who you know is yours, HAMLET.' Come, I'll help you deliver these letters, and quickly too, so you can then take me to the man who sent them.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 7 — Another Room in the Castle
paragraphs: [Enter King and Laertes]
KING. Now your conscience must clear me of guilt, and you must accept me as your friend, since you've heard, with full understanding, that the man who killed your noble father also tried to kill me.

LAERTES. That's clear enough. But tell me — why didn't you take action against these crimes, so serious and so deserving of punishment, when your own safety, wisdom, and every other consideration should have driven you to act?

KING. For two special reasons that may seem weak to you but are strong for me. The Queen, his mother, lives almost entirely for him. And as for myself — whether it's my virtue or my curse — she's so bound up with my life and soul that, like a star that can only move within its sphere, I can't function without her. The other reason I couldn't bring him to public trial is the great love that the common people bear for him. They dip all his faults in their affection, like a spring that turns wood to stone, converting his chains into decorations. My accusations, too lightly made against so powerful a wind of popularity, would have blown right back at me instead of hitting their target.

LAERTES. And so I've lost a noble father, and my sister has been driven to the edge of madness. Her worth — if I may praise what she once was — stood as a challenge to every woman of our age in perfection. But my revenge will come.

KING. Don't lose sleep over it. Don't think we're so dull and lifeless that we'll let our beard be plucked by danger and think it's a game. You'll hear more soon. I loved your father, and we love ourselves — and that, I hope, will lead you to imagine —
[Enter a Messenger]
KING. What's this? What news?
MESSENGER. Letters, my lord, from Hamlet. This one for your Majesty; this one for the Queen.
KING. From Hamlet? Who brought them?
MESSENGER. Sailors, my lord, they said. I didn't see them myself. They were given to me by Claudio, who received them from the man who brought them.
KING. Laertes, you should hear this. Leave us.
[Exit Messenger.]

KING. [Reads.] 'High and Mighty — you should know that I've been set down, stripped of everything, in your kingdom. Tomorrow I'll ask permission to see your royal eyes, at which time, first begging your pardon, I'll explain the circumstances of my sudden and very strange return. HAMLET.' What does this mean? Has everyone else come back too? Or is this some trick, and none of it is real?
LAERTES. Do you recognize the handwriting?
KING. It's Hamlet's writing. 'Stripped of everything!' And in a postscript he says 'alone.' Can you make sense of this?
LAERTES. I'm completely bewildered, my lord. But let him come. It warms the very sickness in my heart to know that I'll get to say to his face: 'This is how you die.'
KING. If that's how it is, Laertes — and how could it not be? — will you let me guide you?
LAERTES. Yes, my lord — as long as you don't try to talk me into making peace.

KING. Into your own peace. If he's actually returned, having abandoned his voyage, and doesn't intend to try again, I'll maneuver him into a plan — one that's fully ripe in my mind — that he won't be able to escape from. And his death will leave no suspicion — even his own mother will consider it an accident.
LAERTES. My lord, I'll follow your lead. Even more so if you could arrange it so that I'm the one who does it.

KING. That works perfectly. You've been talked about a great deal since your travels, and Hamlet heard all of it. There's one particular quality people say you excel in. All your abilities combined didn't make him as envious as this one, which, to my mind, is the least significant.
LAERTES. What quality is that, my lord?

KING. Just a ribbon in the cap of youth, but a necessary one too — because youthful energy is as naturally suited to light and carefree attire as maturity is to dignified clothing. About two months ago, a gentleman from Normandy visited — I've fought against the French myself, and they're superb horsemen — but this fellow seemed to be made one with his horse. He was so extraordinary on horseback that I couldn't even imagine what he did, let alone describe it.
LAERTES. A Norman, was it?
KING. A Norman.
LAERTES. I'd bet my life it was Lamord.
KING. The very same.
LAERTES. I know him well. He's truly the jewel and pride of the whole nation.

KING. He spoke highly of you and gave such a masterful report of your skill in fencing — especially with the rapier — that he declared it would be a sight to see if anyone could match you. The fencers of his own nation, he swore, couldn't touch you in speed, guard, or precision. This report made Hamlet so jealous that all he could do was wish and beg for your quick return so he could fence against you. And out of this —
LAERTES. What comes out of this, my lord?
KING. Laertes, was your father dear to you? Or are you like a painting of sorrow — a face without a heart behind it?
LAERTES. Why do you ask?

KING. Not because I doubt your love. But I know that love begins in time, and I've seen, through clear examples, that time weakens its fire. Within the very flame of love lives a kind of wick that will make it burn lower. Nothing stays good forever — goodness, when it grows too much, dies of its own excess. What we want to do, we should do when we feel like it — because 'want to' changes, and has as many delays and obstacles as there are tongues, hands, and accidents in the world. And then that 'should' becomes like a wasteful sigh — it brings relief but does damage. But let's get to the heart of the matter. Hamlet's back. What would you do to prove yourself your father's true son — in deed, not just in words?
LAERTES. I'd cut his throat in a church.

KING. Indeed, no place should give sanctuary to murder. Revenge should have no limits. But listen, good Laertes — here's what you should do. Stay hidden in your room. When Hamlet returns, he'll learn that you're home. We'll arrange for people to praise your skill, building on the reputation the Frenchman gave you, and bring the two of you together for a match with wagers on the outcome. He's careless, generous, and unsuspecting, so he won't inspect the swords. With a little arrangement, you can easily choose an unblunted blade and, during a practice pass, repay him for your father.

LAERTES. I'll do it. And for that purpose, I'll poison my sword. I bought a deadly ointment from a traveling salesman — so lethal that if you just dip a knife in it, no remedy on earth, no matter how rare, can save the person it scratches. I'll coat the tip of my sword with this poison, so that even the slightest scratch will kill him.

KING. Let's think this through further and consider what timing and circumstances will work best. If this plan fails and our intentions are exposed through poor execution, it would have been better not to try at all. So this scheme should have a backup — a second plan that holds if the first one doesn't work. Let me think. We'll set up a formal wager on your skills — I have it! When the fencing gets intense and you're both hot and thirsty, and he calls for a drink, I'll have a cup prepared for him — a poisoned cup. If he happens to escape your venomous blade, the cup will finish the job.
[Enter Queen]
KING. What is it, dear Queen?
QUEEN. One misery follows right on the heels of another, so fast they come in succession. Your sister has drowned, Laertes.
LAERTES. Drowned! Oh — where?

QUEEN. There's a willow that leans over a brook, showing its silver leaves reflected in the glassy stream. She went there and made wild garlands of wildflowers — crow-flowers, nettles, daisies, and long purples, which country folk give a crude name to, but modest girls call dead men's fingers. Climbing onto the overhanging branches to hang her flower wreaths, a spiteful branch snapped, and she fell, along with her weedy trophies, into the weeping brook. Her clothes spread wide and held her up like a mermaid for a while, during which time she sang snatches of old songs, as if she had no awareness of her own danger — or as if she were a creature born to that element. But it couldn't last long. Her garments, heavy with water, pulled the poor girl from her singing down to a muddy death.
LAERTES. Then she really is drowned?
QUEEN. Drowned, drowned.

LAERTES. You've had too much water already, poor Ophelia — so I'll hold back my tears. But still, it's human nature — let shame say what it will. When these tears are done, the woman in me will be spent. Goodbye, my lord. I have words burning inside me that want to blaze out, but these tears keep drowning them.
[Exit.]
KING. Let's follow him, Gertrude. It was so hard to calm his rage! Now I'm afraid this news will start it all over again. Let's follow him.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 1 — A Churchyard
paragraphs: [Enter two Clowns with spades, &c]
FIRST CLOWN. Is she getting a Christian burial when she deliberately went and drowned herself?
SECOND CLOWN. I'm telling you she is — so dig her grave straight. The coroner held an inquest and ruled it a Christian burial.
FIRST CLOWN. How can that be, unless she drowned herself in self-defense?
SECOND CLOWN. Well, that's what they found.

FIRST CLOWN. It must be 'se offendendo' — it can't be anything else. Here's the point: if I drown myself on purpose, that's an act. And an act has three parts: to act, to do, and to perform. Therefore, she drowned herself on purpose.
SECOND CLOWN. Now hold on, friend —

FIRST CLOWN. Let me finish. Here's the water — good. Here's the man — good. If the man goes to the water and drowns himself, then — like it or not — he goes. Note that. But if the water comes to him and drowns him, he doesn't drown himself. Therefore, the man who isn't responsible for his own death doesn't shorten his own life.
SECOND CLOWN. But is that really the law?
FIRST CLOWN. Absolutely — coroner's inquest law.
SECOND CLOWN. You want the truth? If she hadn't been a gentlewoman, she would have been buried outside the churchyard.

FIRST CLOWN. Exactly right. And the real shame is that important people have more privilege in this world to drown or hang themselves than ordinary Christians do. Come, hand me my spade. There are no true gentlemen except gardeners, ditch-diggers, and grave-makers — they carry on Adam's profession.
SECOND CLOWN. Was Adam a gentleman?
FIRST CLOWN. He was the first person who ever bore arms.
SECOND CLOWN. He didn't have any arms.
FIRST CLOWN. What, are you a heathen? Don't you know your Bible? The Bible says Adam dug. Could he dig without arms? Let me ask you another question. If you can't answer, confess that you —
SECOND CLOWN. Go on then.
FIRST CLOWN. Who builds stronger than the mason, the shipbuilder, or the carpenter?
SECOND CLOWN. The gallows-maker — because that frame outlasts a thousand tenants.

FIRST CLOWN. I like that answer, actually — the gallows does well. But how does it do well? It does well for those who do badly. Now, you're wrong to say the gallows is stronger than the church — therefore the gallows might do well for you. Try again.
SECOND CLOWN. Who builds stronger than a mason, a shipbuilder, or a carpenter?
FIRST CLOWN. That's the question — figure it out.
SECOND CLOWN. Oh, now I've got it.
FIRST CLOWN. Well?
SECOND CLOWN. Hmm — no, I can't figure it out.
[Enter Hamlet and Horatio, at a distance]

FIRST CLOWN. Don't rack your brains about it anymore — beating a dull donkey won't make him go faster. And next time someone asks you that question, say 'a grave-maker.' The houses he builds last until doomsday. Now go — get yourself to the pub and fetch me some beer.
[Exit Second Clown.]
[Digs and sings.]
FIRST CLOWN. In youth when I was in love, in love, I thought it was very sweet. To make a deal, oh, for my advantage, oh, I thought nothing could beat it.
HAMLET. Does this fellow have no feeling for what he's doing? He sings while digging a grave!
HORATIO. Habit has made him completely comfortable with it.
HAMLET. That's how it goes — people who do little hard work have the most sensitive feelings.
[Sings.]
FIRST CLOWN. But age with its creeping steps has caught me in its grip, and shipped me off to the grave, as if I'd never been young at all.
[Throws up a skull.]

HAMLET. That skull had a tongue in it once, and could sing. Look how this fool throws it to the ground, as if it were Cain's jawbone — the one that committed the first murder! This might have been the head of some politician that this gravedigger is now lording over — someone who thought he could outwit God himself. Don't you think?
HORATIO. It might be, my lord.

HAMLET. Or some courtier, who used to say, 'Good morning, sweet lord! How are you, dear lord?' This might have been Lord So-and-so, who praised Lord So-and-so's horse when he really wanted to borrow it. Isn't that possible?
HORATIO. Yes, my lord.

HAMLET. And now it belongs to Lady Worm — jawless, and knocked around with a gravedigger's shovel. Here's a fine revolution, if only we had the insight to see it. Did it cost nothing to raise these bones, only to play bowling with them? My own bones ache to think about it.
[Sings.]
FIRST CLOWN. A pickaxe and a spade, a spade, and also a burial sheet. Oh, a pit of clay must be dug for such a guest so meet.
[Throws up another skull.]

HAMLET. There's another one. Why couldn't that be the skull of a lawyer? Where are his legal tricks now? His subtleties, his cases, his land titles, and his maneuvers? Why does he let this rude gravedigger whack him on the head with a dirty shovel without filing a lawsuit for assault? Hm! This fellow might have been a great buyer of land in his day, with his deeds, his liens, his fines, his double guarantees, and his property claims. Is this the ultimate end of all his legal maneuvering — to have his fine head filled with fine dirt? Will his guarantees guarantee him no more land than the length and width of two legal documents? The very paperwork conveying his property would barely fit in this coffin — and the owner himself gets no more than this?
HORATIO. Not a bit more, my lord.
HAMLET. Isn't parchment made from sheepskins?
HORATIO. Yes, my lord, and from calfskins too.
HAMLET. They are sheep and calves who trust in such things. I'll talk to this fellow. — Whose grave is this, sir?
FIRST CLOWN. Mine, sir.
[Sings.]
FIRST CLOWN. Oh, a pit of clay must be dug for such a guest so meet.
HAMLET. I think it is yours indeed, since you're lying in it.
FIRST CLOWN. You're lying outside it, sir, so it's not yours. As for me, I don't lie in it — yet it's mine.
HAMLET. You do lie in it, since you're in it and say it's yours. It's for the dead, not the living — therefore you're lying.
FIRST CLOWN. That's a quick-footed lie, sir — it'll fly right back from me to you.
HAMLET. What man are you digging it for?
FIRST CLOWN. For no man, sir.
HAMLET. What woman, then?
FIRST CLOWN. For no woman either.
HAMLET. Well, who's going to be buried in it?
FIRST CLOWN. Someone who was a woman, sir, but — rest her soul — she's dead.

HAMLET. How precise this fellow is! We have to speak exactly, or wordplay will undo us. Honestly, Horatio, I've noticed over the past three years — the world has gotten so clever that the common man is practically nipping at the courtier's heels. — How long have you been a gravedigger?
FIRST CLOWN. Of all the days in the year, I started on the very day that our late King Hamlet defeated Fortinbras.
HAMLET. How long ago was that?
FIRST CLOWN. Can't you figure it out? Any fool knows that. It was the very day young Hamlet was born — the one who's gone mad and been sent to England.
HAMLET. Right — why was he sent to England?
FIRST CLOWN. Because he went mad. He'll recover his wits there — or if he doesn't, it won't matter much.
HAMLET. Why not?
FIRST CLOWN. Nobody will notice. Everyone there is as mad as he is.
HAMLET. How did he go mad?
FIRST CLOWN. Very strangely, they say.
HAMLET. How so, strangely?
FIRST CLOWN. Well, by losing his mind.
HAMLET. On what grounds?
FIRST CLOWN. Right here in Denmark. I've been the gravedigger here, man and boy, for thirty years.
HAMLET. How long can a man lie in the earth before he rots?

FIRST CLOWN. Well, if he's not rotten before he dies — and we get a lot of diseased bodies these days that barely hold together for the burial — he'll last you about eight or nine years. A tanner will last nine.
HAMLET. Why longer than others?

FIRST CLOWN. Because, sir, his skin is so toughened by his trade that it keeps water out for a long time. And water is the worst enemy of your dead body. Here's a skull now — this one has been in the ground for twenty-three years.
HAMLET. Whose was it?
FIRST CLOWN. A crazy scoundrel's. Whose do you think?
HAMLET. I have no idea.
FIRST CLOWN. Damn him for a mad fool! He poured a jug of German wine over my head once. This very skull, sir, was Yorick's — the King's jester.
HAMLET. This?
FIRST CLOWN. That very one.

HAMLET. Let me see it. [Takes the skull.] Alas, poor Yorick. I knew him, Horatio — a fellow of infinite humor and the most wonderful imagination. He carried me on his back a thousand times, and now — how disgusting it is to think of! It turns my stomach. Here hung those lips I kissed I don't know how many times. Where are your jokes now? Your tricks? Your songs? Your flashes of wit that used to make the whole table roar with laughter? Not one left to mock your own grinning skull? Completely down in the mouth? Now go to my lady's dressing room and tell her — even if she puts her makeup on an inch thick — she'll end up looking like this. See if that makes her laugh. — Tell me something, Horatio.
HORATIO. What's that, my lord?
HAMLET. Do you think Alexander the Great looked like this when he was in the ground?
HORATIO. Exactly like this.
HAMLET. And smelled like this? Ugh!
[Throws down the skull.]
HORATIO. Exactly like this, my lord.
HAMLET. What lowly uses we return to, Horatio! Can't the imagination follow the noble dust of Alexander until it ends up plugging a beer barrel?
HORATIO. That would be taking the thought too far.

HAMLET. No — not at all. Just follow it logically, with reasonable steps. Alexander died. Alexander was buried. Alexander turned to dust. Dust is earth. From earth we make clay. And why couldn't that clay, which was once Alexander, be used to plug a beer barrel? The mighty Caesar, dead and turned to clay, might stop a hole to keep the wind away. Imagine — the earth that once awed the world now patches a wall against the winter chill! But wait — step aside! Here comes the King.
[Enter priests, &c, in procession; the corpse of Ophelia, Laertes and]

HAMLET. Mourners following; King, Queen, their Trains, &c. The Queen, the courtiers — who is it they're following? And with such a cut-short ceremony? This suggests the body they're following took its own life. It must have been someone of rank. Let's hide and watch.
[Retiring with Horatio.]
LAERTES. What other ceremony is there?
HAMLET. That's Laertes — a very noble young man. Watch.
LAERTES. What other ceremony?

PRIEST. The funeral rites have been extended as far as we're authorized to allow. Her death was suspicious, and if not for the King's overriding command, she would have been buried in unconsecrated ground until Judgment Day. Instead of prayers, stones and pebbles should have been thrown on her. Yet she has been allowed her maiden rites — her virgin flowers and the church bells and burial ceremony.
LAERTES. Can nothing more be done?
PRIEST. No. We would dishonor the service for the dead if we sang a solemn requiem and gave her the same rest we give to those who died in peace.

LAERTES. Lay her in the earth, and from her fair and unspoiled flesh may violets grow. I tell you, you heartless priest — my sister will be a ministering angel in heaven while you lie howling in hell.
HAMLET. What — the beautiful Ophelia?
QUEEN. [Scattering flowers.] Sweets for the sweet. Farewell. I had hoped you would be my Hamlet's wife. I thought I'd decorate your bridal bed, sweet girl, not scatter flowers on your grave.
LAERTES. Oh, let triple sorrow fall ten times over on the cursed head whose wicked act robbed you of your brilliant mind! Hold off the earth a while, until I've held her once more in my arms.
[Leaps into the grave.]
LAERTES. Now pile the dirt on the living and the dead, until you've made a mountain out of this flat ground — taller than Mount Pelion or the sky-reaching peak of blue Olympus.
[Advancing.]
HAMLET. Who is this, whose grief is so extreme? Whose passionate words could make the stars stop and stare in wonder? It is I — Hamlet the Dane!
[Leaps into the grave.]
LAERTES. [Grappling with him.] The devil take your soul!
HAMLET. That's a poor prayer. Please take your fingers off my throat. I may not be quick to anger, but I have something dangerous in me — your wisdom should fear it. Let go of me!
KING. Pull them apart!
QUEEN. Hamlet! Hamlet! All. Gentlemen!
HORATIO. My lord, calm yourself.
[The Attendants part them, and they come out of the grave.]
HAMLET. I'll fight him on this subject until my eyelids can't move anymore!
QUEEN. Oh, my son — what subject?
HAMLET. I loved Ophelia. Forty thousand brothers, with all their love combined, could not match mine. What will you do for her?
KING. Oh — he's mad, Laertes.
QUEEN. For the love of God, leave him alone!

HAMLET. By God, show me what you'll do! Will you weep? Will you fight? Will you starve yourself? Will you tear yourself apart? Will you drink vinegar? Eat a crocodile? I'll match anything. Did you come here to whine? To outdo me by leaping into her grave? Be buried alive with her — so will I! And if you want to talk about piling mountains on us, let them throw millions of acres on top of us until the ground scorches the sky. If you're going to rant, I can rant just as well as you.
QUEEN. This is pure madness. The fit will work on him for a while, and then, as patient as a dove sitting on her golden eggs, his calm will return.

HAMLET. Listen, sir — what reason do you have for treating me this way? I always cared for you. But it doesn't matter. Let Hercules himself do his best — the cat will meow, and every dog will have his day.
[Exit.]
KING. Horatio, please go with him.
[Exit Horatio.]
[To Laertes]

KING. Hold to the patience we agreed on in our conversation last night. We'll put this matter into action soon. — Gertrude, have someone keep watch over your son. This grave will have a lasting monument. We'll have an hour of calm before long — until then, let's be patient in what we do.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 2 — A Hall in the Castle
paragraphs: [Enter Hamlet and Horatio]
HAMLET. So much for that business, sir. Now let me tell you the other part. You remember everything that happened?
HORATIO. Of course, my lord!

HAMLET. Sir, there was a kind of battle going on inside me that wouldn't let me sleep. I felt worse than prisoners in chains. But then — and I praise rashness for this — let's acknowledge that sometimes acting without thinking serves us well, when our careful plans fail. And that should teach us that there's a divine power that shapes how things turn out, no matter how roughly we hack at them ourselves.
HORATIO. That's absolutely true.

HAMLET. I got up from my bunk, wrapped my sea-cloak around me, and groped through the dark to find them. I got hold of their packet, stole back to my own cabin — my fear overriding my manners — and broke open their official commission. There, Horatio, I found — oh, royal treachery! — an exact order, padded with all kinds of reasons about Denmark's well-being and England's too, with such terrifying descriptions of what a danger I was that, upon reading it, without any delay — not even time to sharpen the axe — my head was to be struck off.
HORATIO. Is that possible?
HAMLET. Here's the commission — read it at your leisure. But do you want to hear what I did next?
HORATIO. Please tell me.

HAMLET. Surrounded on all sides by this treachery — before I could even think of a plan, my hands had already started acting — I sat down and wrote a new commission in a fair hand. I used to think, like politicians do, that good handwriting was beneath me, and I worked hard to forget what I'd learned. But now, sir, it served me well. Do you want to know what I wrote?
HORATIO. Yes, my lord.

HAMLET. An urgent command from the King, saying that — since England was a faithful ally of Denmark, since their friendship should flourish like a palm tree, since peace should forever stand between them wearing her crown of wheat — and many other such formal phrases of great weight — that upon reading this document, without any further discussion, the bearers of this letter should be immediately put to death. No time for confession allowed.
HORATIO. How did you seal it?

HAMLET. Even that worked out by heaven's design. I had my father's signet ring in my pocket — it was the model for the Danish royal seal. I folded the new letter to look like the old one, signed it, stamped it with the seal, and put it back safely. The switch was never detected. The next day came our sea battle — and what followed after that, you already know.
HORATIO. So Rosencrantz and Guildenstern are heading to their deaths.

HAMLET. Well, they embraced this assignment eagerly. They're not on my conscience. Their downfall is their own doing. It's dangerous when people of lesser character insert themselves between the fierce, clashing swords of powerful enemies.
HORATIO. What a king this Claudius is!

HAMLET. Don't you think it's now my moral obligation — he who killed my king and seduced my mother, who slipped in between me and the throne, who tried to have me killed by trickery — isn't it a matter of perfect conscience to strike him down with this arm? And isn't it damnable to let this cancer of our nature continue to grow and do more evil?
HORATIO. He'll find out soon enough from England what happened to Rosencrantz and Guildenstern.

HAMLET. It won't be long. The time in between is mine. And killing a man takes no longer than saying 'one.' But I'm truly sorry, good Horatio, that I lost my temper with Laertes. In the image of his cause, I see a reflection of my own. I'll try to win his favor. But his extravagant show of grief pushed me into a towering rage.
HORATIO. Quiet — who's coming?
[Enter Osric]
OSRIC. Your lordship is most welcome back to Denmark.
HAMLET. Thank you kindly, sir. Do you know this butterfly?
HORATIO. No, my lord.

HAMLET. Good for you — knowing him is no virtue. He owns a lot of fertile land. Let an animal be lord of animals, and his feeding trough will stand at the king's table. He's a jackdaw — but, as I said, well-supplied with dirt.
OSRIC. Sweet lord, if your lordship has a moment, I'd like to pass along a message from his Majesty.
HAMLET. I'm all ears. Put your hat back on — it belongs on your head.
OSRIC. Thank you, my lord — it's very hot.
HAMLET. No, trust me — it's very cold. The wind is from the north.
OSRIC. It is rather cold, my lord, now that you mention it.
HAMLET. Actually, I think it's very humid and hot for my constitution.
OSRIC. Extremely hot, my lord — terribly sultry, as it were — I can't quite say how. But, my lord, his Majesty asked me to tell you he's placed a large wager on your head. Sir, here's the matter —
HAMLET. Please, remember your hat —
[Hamlet moves him to put on his hat.]

OSRIC. No really, my lord — I'm fine without it. Sir, Laertes has recently arrived at court — believe me, an absolute gentleman, full of the most excellent qualities, with very refined manners and an impressive presence. Indeed, to speak accurately of him, he is the very model of gentlemanly behavior — because you'd find in him every quality a gentleman could wish to see.

HAMLET. Sir, your description of him loses nothing in your delivery, though I know that to catalog his virtues individually would overwhelm the capacity of memory and still only zigzag behind his actual excellence. But in honest praise, I consider him a person of great substance and of such rare and precious quality that, to truly describe him, his only true likeness is his mirror — and anyone who tried to follow his example would be nothing more than his shadow.
OSRIC. Your lordship describes him perfectly.
HAMLET. But what's the point, sir? Why are we wrapping this gentleman in our crude words?
OSRIC. Sir?
HORATIO. Wouldn't it be possible to say all this in plain language? You could do it, sir, really.
HAMLET. What is the purpose of bringing up this gentleman?
OSRIC. Laertes?
HORATIO. His vocabulary is spent — all his golden words have been used up.
HAMLET. Yes, him.
OSRIC. I know you're aware —
HAMLET. I wish you were right about that, sir. Though honestly, even if you were, it wouldn't be much to my credit. Well, sir?
OSRIC. You're surely not unaware of what an excellent swordsman Laertes is —
HAMLET. I wouldn't dare claim that, in case it sounded like I was comparing myself to him in excellence. But to truly know a man, you'd have to know yourself first.
OSRIC. I mean, sir, with his weapon. But his reputation is that he's unmatched.
HAMLET. What's his weapon?
OSRIC. Rapier and dagger.
HAMLET. That's two of his weapons. But go on.

OSRIC. The King, sir, has wagered six Barbary horses against him. Laertes has put up, as I understand it, six French rapiers and daggers, with their accessories — belts, hangers, and so on. Three of the sword-hangers are especially beautiful — very elegant, richly designed, and of very refined craftsmanship.
HAMLET. What do you mean by 'hangers'?
HORATIO. I knew he'd need a footnote before he was done.
OSRIC. The hangers, sir, are the sword-belt straps.
