HAMLET. The word 'carriages' would fit better if we could carry cannons on our hips. Until then, let's call them hangers. But go on — six Barbary horses against six French swords with their accessories, including three fancy hangers. That's the French bet against the Danish one. Why has all this been wagered?

OSRIC. The King, sir, has bet that in a dozen passes between you and Laertes, he won't beat you by more than three hits. The ratio is twelve to nine. And the match could happen right now if your lordship would agree to participate.
HAMLET. What if I say no?
OSRIC. I mean, my lord, your personal participation in the fencing match.

HAMLET. Sir, I'll be walking here in the hall. If it suits his Majesty, this is my usual time for exercise. Let the swords be brought. If the gentleman is willing and the King holds to his plan, I'll try to win for him if I can. If not, I'll get nothing but my shame and a few hits against me.
OSRIC. Shall I report your answer exactly like that?
HAMLET. That's the gist of it, sir. Add whatever fancy flourishes your nature requires.
OSRIC. I present my humble service to your lordship.
HAMLET. Yours, yours.
[Exit Osric.]
HAMLET. He does well to commend himself — no one else would do it for him.
HORATIO. This young bird ran off with eggshell still on his head.

HAMLET. He was probably this polite to his mother's breast before he was weaned. He's like many others I know in this lazy age — they've picked up the trendy tone and the fashionable manners of the time. It's a superficial, frothy collection of phrases that carries them through the most refined society. But test them, and the bubbles burst.
[Enter a Lord]
LORD. My lord, his Majesty sent word through young Osric that you're expected in the hall. He wants to know if you're still willing to fence with Laertes, or if you need more time.
HAMLET. My plans haven't changed — I follow the King's schedule. If he's ready, so am I. Now or whenever, as long as I'm in the shape I'm in now.
LORD. The King and Queen and everyone are on their way down.
HAMLET. Good timing.
LORD. The Queen asks that you be friendly and gracious toward Laertes before you begin fencing.
HAMLET. That's good advice.
[Exit Lord.]
HORATIO. You're going to lose this match, my lord.

HAMLET. I don't think so. Since he went to France, I've been practicing constantly. I'll win at the odds they've set. But you wouldn't believe how uneasy I feel around my heart — though it doesn't matter.
HORATIO. No, my lord —
HAMLET. It's foolishness — but it's the kind of foreboding that might trouble a woman.
HORATIO. If your instinct warns you against something, obey it. I'll tell them you're not feeling well and postpone the match.

HAMLET. Not at all — we defy omens. There's a special providence even in the fall of a sparrow. If it's going to happen now, it won't happen later. If it won't happen later, it will happen now. If it's not now, it will come eventually. Being ready is everything. Since no one knows what they're leaving behind, what does it matter to leave early?
[Enter King, Queen, Laertes, Lords, Osric and Attendants with foils &c]
KING. Come, Hamlet — come take this hand from me.
[The King puts Laertes's hand into Hamlet's.]

HAMLET. Give me your pardon, sir. I've wronged you. But forgive me, as a gentleman would. Everyone here knows, and you must have heard, how I've been punished with a terrible madness. What I did that might have offended your feelings, your honor, and your sense of what's right — I declare here that it was madness. Was it Hamlet who wronged Laertes? Never. If Hamlet is taken away from himself, and when he's not himself does wrong to Laertes, then Hamlet doesn't do it — Hamlet denies it. Who does it, then? His madness. If that's the case, Hamlet belongs to the wronged party — his madness is poor Hamlet's enemy. Sir, before this audience, let my disclaimer of any intentional evil free me, at least in your generous mind, from blame — as if I had shot an arrow over a roof and accidentally hit my brother.

LAERTES. My natural feelings are satisfied — and those should be the strongest drive toward revenge. But in terms of my honor, I hold back and won't make peace until I've consulted with respected authorities to ensure my reputation isn't damaged. But until then, I accept your offered friendship as genuine, and I won't do anything to wrong it.
HAMLET. I accept that freely, and I'll enter into this brotherly contest without any hidden agenda. Give us the swords. Come on.
LAERTES. Come — one for me.
HAMLET. I'll serve as a foil to you, Laertes — against my background of ignorance, your skill will shine like a star in the darkest night.
LAERTES. You're mocking me, sir.
HAMLET. No, I swear it.
KING. Give them the swords, young Osric. Nephew Hamlet — you know the wager?
HAMLET. Very well, my lord. Your Majesty has bet on the weaker side.
KING. I'm not worried. I've seen you both fence. But since he's the better swordsman, we've given him the handicap.
LAERTES. This one is too heavy. Let me try another.
HAMLET. This one suits me fine. Are they all the same length?
[They prepare to play.]
OSRIC. Yes, my lord.

KING. Set the wine cups on that table. If Hamlet scores the first or second hit, or ties on the third exchange, let all the cannons on the battlements fire. The King will drink to Hamlet's improved performance, and into the cup he'll drop a precious pearl, richer than any worn by four successive Danish kings. Give me the cups — and let the drum signal the trumpet, the trumpet signal the cannon outside, the cannon signal the heavens, and the heavens echo back to earth: 'Now the King drinks to Hamlet!' Come, begin. And you judges, watch carefully.
HAMLET. Come on, sir.
LAERTES. Come, my lord.
[They play.]
HAMLET. One!
LAERTES. No.
HAMLET. Judge?
OSRIC. A hit — a very clear hit.
LAERTES. Fine — again.
KING. Wait — give me something to drink. Hamlet, this pearl is yours. Here's to your health.
[Trumpets sound, and cannon shot off within.]
KING. Give him the cup.
HAMLET. I'll finish this round first — set it aside for now.
[They play.]
HAMLET. Come on — another hit! What do you say?
LAERTES. I admit it — a touch.
KING. Our son will win.
QUEEN. He's out of shape and short of breath. Here, Hamlet, take my handkerchief and wipe your forehead. The Queen drinks to your success, Hamlet.
HAMLET. Thank you, madam.
KING. Gertrude — don't drink!
QUEEN. I will, my lord — excuse me.
KING. [Aside.] It's the poisoned cup! It's too late.
HAMLET. I don't dare drink yet, madam. In a moment.
QUEEN. Come, let me wipe your face.
LAERTES. My lord, I'll hit him now.
KING. I don't think so.
LAERTES. [Aside.] And yet it's almost against my conscience.
HAMLET. Come, Laertes — the third round. You're just playing around. Give me your best effort, please. I'm afraid you're going easy on me.
LAERTES. You think so? Come on, then.
[They play.]
OSRIC. Nothing scored on either side.
LAERTES. Take that! [Laertes wounds Hamlet; then, in scuffling, they change rapiers, and Hamlet wounds Laertes.]
KING. Pull them apart — they're getting violent!
HAMLET. No — come on, again!
[The Queen falls.]
OSRIC. Look to the Queen!
HORATIO. They're both bleeding! How are you, my lord?
OSRIC. How are you, Laertes?
LAERTES. Like a bird caught in my own trap, Osric. I'm justly killed by my own treachery.
HAMLET. How is the Queen?
KING. She fainted at the sight of blood.
QUEEN. No, no — the drink, the drink! Oh my dear Hamlet — the drink, the drink! I've been poisoned!
[Dies.]
HAMLET. Villainy! Lock the doors! Treachery! Find out who's responsible!
[Laertes falls.]

LAERTES. It's right here, Hamlet. You are killed. No medicine in the world can save you. You have less than half an hour to live. The treacherous weapon is in your hand — unblunted and poisoned. The foul plot has turned on me. Here I lie, never to rise again. Your mother has been poisoned. I can't go on. The King — the King is to blame.
HAMLET. The blade is poisoned too? Then, poison — do your work!
[Stabs the King.]
HAMLET. OSRIC and LORDS. Treason! Treason!
KING. Oh — defend me, friends! I'm only wounded!
HAMLET. Here, you incestuous, murderous, damned Dane — drink this potion! Is your precious pearl in there? Follow my mother!
[King dies.]
LAERTES. He got what he deserved. It was a poison he prepared himself. Exchange forgiveness with me, noble Hamlet. May my death and my father's death not be held against you, nor yours against me.
[Dies.]

HAMLET. May heaven forgive you. I follow you. I am dead, Horatio. Wretched Queen, farewell. You who stand there, pale and trembling at this spectacle — you who are nothing but silent witnesses to this act — if I only had time, since this harsh officer, Death, is strict in making his arrest — oh, I could tell you — but let it go. Horatio, I am dead. You live. Tell my story and explain my cause truthfully to those who don't understand.
HORATIO. Don't believe I'll do that. I'm more like an ancient Roman than a Dane. There's still some poison left in that cup.

HAMLET. If you're truly my friend, give me the cup! Let it go — by heaven, I'll have it! Oh, good Horatio, what a damaged reputation I'll leave behind if things remain unexplained. If you ever held me in your heart, stay away from happiness a while longer and endure the pain of this harsh world — to tell my story.
[March afar off, and shot within.]
HAMLET. What's that warlike sound?
OSRIC. Young Fortinbras, returning victorious from Poland, is firing a salute to honor the English ambassadors.

HAMLET. Oh — I'm dying, Horatio. The powerful poison is overwhelming me. I won't live to hear the news from England. But I predict the election will fall on Fortinbras. He has my dying vote. Tell him everything that has led to this — the major events and the minor ones. The rest is silence.
[Dies.]
HORATIO. Now a noble heart has broken. Good night, sweet prince — and may flights of angels sing you to your rest. Why is that drumbeat approaching?
[March within.]
[Enter Fortinbras, the English Ambassadors and others]
FORTINBRAS. Where is this sight?
HORATIO. What are you looking for? If it's sorrow or wonder, look no further.
FORTINBRAS. This heap of dead bodies calls out for blood. Oh proud Death, what feast are you preparing in your eternal hall, that you've struck down so many princes at once, so bloodily?

FIRST AMBASSADOR. The sight is horrifying. And our news from England comes too late. The ears that should hear us are now deaf. We came to tell the King that his command has been carried out — Rosencrantz and Guildenstern are dead. Where do we get our thanks?

HORATIO. Not from his lips, even if he were still alive to give them. He never ordered their deaths. But since you've all arrived at this bloody moment — you from the wars in Poland, and you from England — give orders for these bodies to be placed on a high platform for everyone to see. And let me tell the world, which doesn't yet know, how all of this happened. You'll hear about unnatural bloodshed, accidental judgments, casual killings, deaths caused by cunning and necessity, and plans gone wrong that fell on the heads of those who made them. All of this I can truthfully recount.

FORTINBRAS. Let's hear it quickly, and summon the noblest people to listen. As for me, I embrace my fortune with sorrow. I have some inherited rights to this kingdom, and now seems the time to claim them.

HORATIO. I have reason to speak about that too — and from the mouth of one whose voice will carry great weight. But let all of this be done immediately, while people's minds are still in turmoil, before more disasters can follow from confusion and misunderstanding.

FORTINBRAS. Let four captains carry Hamlet to the stage like a soldier, because he was likely, had he been given the chance, to have proved himself most royally. And for his final passage, let the soldiers' music and the military honors speak loudly for him. Pick up the bodies. A sight like this belongs on a battlefield, not here — it looks terribly wrong in a court. Give the order for the soldiers to fire their guns.
[A dead march.]
[Exeunt, bearing off the bodies, after which a peal of ordnance is shot off.]
